utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I -- first I would like to inform the parties that on the basis of the submissions made as far as time is concerned, that we need a full afternoon session if we want to finish with this witness. And also in view of what was submitted by the Stanisic Defence yesterday, the Chamber has decided that we'll sit this afternoon as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just inform Your Honours that the medical service -- sorry, let me put it differently. Mr. Stanisic will have to see the medical service this afternoon. He's been told that he will be transported back to UNDU around the time of the end of what would be the normal session. But as I indicated yesterday, we can proceed in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's understood. And I don't know whether we need an official waiver form or whether your -- the submission you just made, that Mr. Stanisic waives his right to be present in court at times today, when he will go back to the UNDU where we have an extended session, whether that -- I think that would be sufficient. Because the forms mainly serve at moments where the accused is not in a courtroom itself and that the Chamber needs to -- needs written evidence that they can proceed, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, could I just have one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just consult, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There's no difference, that Mr. Stanisic waives his right to be present this afternoon in the event that he has to go to the doctor's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Or the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Unless there's any other matter. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And we arranged for a hearing this afternoon as well so that there's a fair chance that we could conclude your testimony, although later, but still today. Mr. Jordash, if you're read, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me just pick up quickly where we left off yesterday concerning the relationship between the Serbian DB and Arkan's Tigers. A witness in this courtroom testified that they had been present at certain points during the Pauk operation and had observed a strained relationship between men who were associated with the Serbian DB and some of Arkan's Men. That's a witness who was called Lazarevic. Did you observe such a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. Page 3375 -- sorry, no. Page 3411 to 3415.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He said that -- and I'll just give you a bit more detail. He said that he never saw the men from the DB socialised with Arkan's men and they had a strained relationship because Arkan's men had a poor reputation. Did you observe a strained relationship between men associated with the Serbian DB and Arkan's men, the men who joined the Pauk operation? Are you able to testify about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I said I -- I have already said I wasn't in the area of Velika Kladusa, so I don't know who associated with whom. But I do agree the relationship between Arkan's men and the DB wasn't a good one. I would say that the DB, the state security, however, had a bad reputation. I wouldn't agree with the claim that Arkan's Tigers had a bad reputation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move to a related subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have D273 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some activities concerning weapons supply in 1991 and whether you now anything about this. Perhaps before the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sorry, this is a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps before this comes up on the screen, you would -- I can shortcut things by asking you this: Have you ever heard of the Zukanovics brothers? Zukanovic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about Arkan taking weapons from a TO depot in Lipovica in 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about weapons being transported by members of the Delije, one of Arkan's companies? Did you ever hear about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which period you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that Arkan, given what he said, and given what the public would say, in Serbia, at the beginning of 1991 he attempted to transport some weapons to Knin, but he was arrested in Dvor na Uni and spent six months in prison in Zagreb. That is the only thing I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'll leave that subject then. I don't think we need to look at this exhibit, since you don't seem to have any information, or relevant information. Let's move on to a different subject. The attack on Bijeljina. You testified on the 24th of January - and let me try to read the relevant piece of it, testimony, so that you can recall what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 16347.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You testified as follows: "Immediately after the call from Biljana Plavsic, there was contact -- contact was established with our people in Bijeljina. And our member whose nickname is Mauzer told us that it was absolutely necessary for the guards to go and liberate Bijeljina." And you were asked the question by Mr. Bakrac: "After your arrival there, did you find out from Arkan or from someone else, did you find out whether the guards participated in the liberation of Bijeljina on an independent basis, or were they provided with support of some kind? And if so, with what kind of support? "The guards had two forms of support. They were supported by our members led by Mauzer. "But the main form of support was in the form of logistics, and it was provided by the army, an army garrison in Bijeljina. Major Gavrilovic commanded that garrison and he later became the commander of the 2nd Semberija Brigade." And a bit further down: "So the army provided us with logistics support ..." Did all the logistics from that -- for that attack come from the army, or did you have any other form of support, in terms of logistics?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All logistics support was provided by the army garrison in Bijeljina under the command of Major Gavrilovic. Our volunteers slept over there and received food, so it wasn't necessary to have any other form of combat support, since the operation only took a day. So the army didn't get involved. But an agreement had been previously reached, according to which the army would provide artillery support and all other forms of support for the guards. But all of that, in the end, was not necessary, since the operation was rapidly completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did they provide some form of weapons or ammunition?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You said: "So the army provided us with logistics support, but the agreement was that the army should provide us with full combat support as well. But since we co-operated very successfully with the local patriots and groups, it wasn't --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down when reading, for the benefit of the B/C/S booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. "... it wasn't necessary for the Army of Yugoslavia to get involved in the conflict."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you did say on the 24th of January that the army provided you with logistics support. Are you suggesting now they didn't?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I have said, the army provided us with logistic support. We slept over on their premises and our combatants received food from them. But, as I said, military support, combat support, was not necessary in the end, although, according to the agreement reached, they had intended to provide us with such support.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: After the operation was completed, the Tigers returned to the army barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And continued to plan the next stage of the operation with the army.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Biljana Plavsic requested that Zvornik be liberated as well. And that operation was also carried out together with the Army of Yugoslavia. The army corps was headed by General Savo Jankovic. We had full logistics and combat support in Zvornik because, at the time, the guards who were present on the occasion of the liberation of Zvornik numbered about 60 men, so they provided military support to liberate Zvornik, because the guards, with so few men, was not in a position to liberate a town as big as Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So from what you've said, this was -- these two operations were the results of a very closely tied co-ordination between Arkan's Men and the army. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was their subordination ultimately of Arkan's men to the army; or was it co-ordination of two equal partners?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it was the Army of Yugoslavia and not the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, it was a matter of acting as partners or as using our forces as joint forces. Using the forces of the army and the SDG as joint forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'd like to ask one question to seek further clarification of the previous testimony which you touched upon as well. Witness, you were asked by Mr. Bakrac the part that was read by Mr. Jordash; that is, a call from Biljana Plavsic, then Mauzer telling that it was absolutely necessary for the guards to go and liberate Bijeljina. Then, From whom did you get support? And you started that answer by: "The guards had two forms of support. They were supported by our members led by Mauzer ..." Now, you introduced Mauzer as one of your members. That sounds as the guards receiving support from the guards. Therefore, I have some difficulties in understanding what, then, those men were, your members led by Mauzer. Were they there already? What does that mean, "getting support from your own people"? I would not call that support, but ... could you explain that a bit more in detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I have already said, Mauzer was a member of ours, but not other men and the TO members in Bijeljina that he had assembled. So his support and the support of those Territorial Defence members was very important for us. He was a member of ours. We only had one member there. Later, another member became included. But at the time it was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I now understand. If you say, "They were supported by our members led by Mauzer," there were not other members led by Mauzer because Mauzer was the only one who was there. And you said later there was another one. There -- another member became included at the time. So it was your men being called for the liberation of Bijeljina, were supported by Mauzer and one other member who was there together with Mauzer, and a group of men led by Mauzer, although not members of the Guard. Is that -- but coming from TO, et cetera. Is that how I have to understand the line "They were supported by our members led by Mauzer"? Most of them were not your members.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the men led by Mauzer, these -- as I understand it, these were TO members. Did the TO members receive their logistics, i.e., weapons and ammunition, from the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain that all these people were members of the Territorial Defence in Bijeljina. I know there were some members of the Serbian Radical Party from Bijeljina as well. As to whether they personally received army support, support from the Army of Yugoslavia, I really don't know. I know that Arkan told me that they, that's the Serbian Volunteer Guard, received logistics support from the JNA, from the garrison, with Major Gavrilovic at its head. But as for whether these other people received such support, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the -- thank you for the answer, Mr. Witness. In relation to Zvornik, is this correct: That the conflict there erupted in the evening of the 8th of April, 1992, and it erupted when elements of the JNA, 336th Motorised Brigade, the Volunteer Guards, and TO units seized control of the town? Does that summarize your understanding of how the Zvornik attack took place?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, if I understood you properly, you asked me whether the conflict started when the joint JNA forces, the Territorial Defence, and the guards attacked Zvornik. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know, again, whether there was subordination of these three groups, or were they acting as equal partners?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can talk about is the relationship between the army and the SDG. I don't know whether the Territorial Defence was subordinated to somebody. As for the JNA and the SDG, they were partners. They acted in concert.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you come across or hear about Captain Dragan Obrenovic commanding a battalion of the JNA involved in that attack?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I wasn't there, I can say that the only person that Arkan mentioned was Commander Sava Jankovic, with whom Arkan co-operated closely. I didn't hear of the other person, the captain that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just -- just -- perhaps I've missed this, but just so that we're clear: The information that you have about Zvornik and Bijeljina came directly from Arkan contemporaneously, i.e., as things were happening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was at the Krka monastery, and at the time we did not have direct means of communication. I only heard about those things later. I did not have any information at the time, save for those things that I saw when I was in the monastery and when I watched the main TV news.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's break that down again. But you did hear these things from Arkan; is that correct? Directly from Arkan.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you heard about them the next time you saw Arkan after the operation. How long after these operations did Arkan tell you these things?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about those things when I returned to Erdut from the monastery. Sometime past thereafter, perhaps half a year, or perhaps even a year, because our relationship at the time was not of such a nature that he should immediately tell me everything about what had transpired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Let's move to a different subject. P --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, P1127.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is a one of the documents I hope you looked at yesterday, so hopefully we can keep things short. Did you see this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. You provided the document to me with the Court's approval, I read it, and I, more or less, understood what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the formation of this special-purpose unit called the Red Tigers being part of the 101st RSK MUP Training Centre led by Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A distinction should be made between two things. That unit was not under Arkan's command, but the 101st Centre was, indeed, under Arkan's command. And I believe that that's what this agent meant, what he had in mind when he wrote to the DB chief. This doesn't mean that Arkan was the commander of the Red Tigers. He was the commander of the 101st Centre. That unit was supposed to have been billeted in our centre, but that never transpired. It would not have been logical. It says here that the unit was close to the communist organisation, or, rather, the new party known as JUL. This would have been completely ruled out, because we were that party's political opponents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, could you please speak a bit slower because the interpreters have difficulties in following your speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's move on to, then, D398, under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This was also a document I hope you saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we can see what it is on the screen. And I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, page 2 of the English and 2 of the B/C/S. Actually, 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the report notes -- or the report speaks of the RSK MUP staff being dismissed or an attempt to dismiss them. And that attempt being supported by Arkan and Milovanovic, the RSK assistant minister for national defence, and the meeting being attended by Bozik [phoen], who was the vice premier of the RSK, who disagreed with the attempt to remove the RSK MUP officials. Is this something you can testify to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just -- I know that the transcript probably reflects what was said, but that the document says "Stevo Bogic," not "Bozik," as reflected on 13, line 7. Just for later references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's hereby on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is this something you know about: The dispute between RSK officials on the one side, and Arkan and Mrgud on the other in early -- well, late 1992, I suggest, and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the document yesterday. It arises from -- from it that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and Milan Milanovic, Mrgud, were against some of the elements of the RSK MUP that co-operated with the DB from Belgrade. It is stated clearly here that Milomir Ljubovic should replace Kojic and that Ivko -- Slobodan Ivkovic, who was accused of co-operating with the DB department of Serbia should have been replaced, and this clearly transpires from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I -- we can see what transpires from the document. What I'm trying to ask you about is whether you have any independent knowledge. It's our case, you see, that there was a dispute between RSK MUP officials and particularly Ilija Kojic and Arkan. Ilija Kojic on the one side, Arkan and Mrgud on the other. Is that something you can testify to? We know what the document says. The document confirms that. But can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a dispute, indeed. Mr. Kojic relied too heavily on the DB department of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When did this dispute begin, according to you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How long did it continue?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Perhaps a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did Arkan and Mrgud and also Hadzic attempt to remove Kojic and other RSK MUP officials?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this one of the reasons that Arkan was so against the Serbian DB? He felt as though they were using people like Kojic to work against his objectives.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. However, when it comes to those objectives, I have to say that Arkan's objective was primarily to unite all of the Serbian lands and the Serbian people in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Obviously the DB was against those objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just let me try to, if I can, understand this. What do you mean that Arkan's objective was to unite all the Serbian lands and the Serbian people? What does that mean in real terms, in terms of territory?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In real terms at the time, that meant that Republika Srpska, the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and the eastern and western parts were to be united with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Through the creation of Serb territories all linked up between these three places. Is that -- is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you say: "Obviously the DB was against these objectives." What makes you -- what made you conclude -- did you conclude that at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conclude that based on the then-position of the president of Serbia, which was at that time Yugoslavia, Mr. Slobodan Milosevic. And obviously the DB had to comply with his orders. There was a time when he imposed a blockade between the Republic of Serbia and Republika Srpska. Everybody had to obey him, and that was the main difference between us and them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How -- how was it that Kojic acted against those objectives such that Arkan wanted to get rid of him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the details. However, I'm sure that there were reasons good enough to remove him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you conclude that because Arkan was sufficiently forceful or aggressive in his attempts to remove Kojic; is that -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not just Arkan. It was a joint position adopted by Hadzic and Milan Milanovic, Mrgud. The three of them wanted to remove Kojic and the gentlemen from the DB who co-operated closely with the DB of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now - is this right? - this was at the time or certainly around the time when the Vance Plan, or certainty the dispute then was around the time, or began around the time that the Vance Plan had been -- or was beginning to be implemented; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the PJMs had been formed within the RSK; is that right? The police brigades.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There's been a suggestion in this case that around that time that, in fact, Kojic commanded Arkan; that Arkan was subordinated to Kojic. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the Serbian Volunteer Guards, after the Vance Plan was implemented, had to be transformed into the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, in that sense, that would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But in real terms, in terms of day-to-day command, that's not correct. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, moving forward a little bit in time, in terms of -- by the time we arrive in -- into, say, 1994, 1994, are you aware of a Joint Defence Council existing between the RSK officials and the Republika Srpska officials? Probably a little later than that, maybe late 1994, a Joint Defence Council dealing with joint defence operations between the Bosnian Serbs and the RSK Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How did it -- do you know anything about how it worked? What it meant, in real terms? On a day-to-day operational kind of level.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already told you, the Serbian Volunteer Guards units were sent to Velika Kladusa in November 1994, based on an agreement that was reached by Milosevic, Martic, Karadzic, and Fikret Abdic. The example clearly shows that there was, indeed, quite a lot of co-operation between the Republika Srpska officials and the officials of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So is this right: As a result of that agreement, battalions of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina would be sent to the Republika Srpska on a monthly basis to assist the Republika Srpska and their military objectives?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question because I don't know anything about that. The only thing I know about are the activities of the SDG in Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. But I've already spoken about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'm not going to push you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just take instructions? I think I may have finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Weber, are you ready? Mr. Pelevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, to begin: At transcript pages 16364 to 16366, the Simatovic Defence played a five-minute video of a speech by Arkan from the end of 1992 where he refers to the united states of Serbia. This video has not been tendered. At this time, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 2D1001 with transcripts available under 2D1001.1 as a public exhibit. For the record, this speech has also been referenced in the transcript as 65 ter 6314.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it intentionally that you did not tender it, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. It was my mistake. Yesterday I did not tender the document into evidence after it was exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two observations: First, the video is not in the system of the Registrar, so that is one. Second, if it would be, would it then not be more cautious to give an opportunity to Mr. Bakrac to tender it because he was the one who introduced it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I was mainly addressing it as a housekeeping item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, if you would take care that the video is in the system, then it can be admitted into evidence. Of course, since it is played, it's always traceable what was shown. But if it's not in the e-court system, then, of course, it's not admitted into evidence. You cannot rely on it other than that it was played.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my Case Manager is dealing with that as we speak. We were told to prepare everything, to put everything in place to be able to upload it into the system today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we wait for your further activity. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On Tuesday, you were shown a video of a speech by Arkan where he refers to the creation of the united states of Serbia. You stated that this speech was at the Sava conference hall. Was the location where this speech took place in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Sava conference hall is in Belgrade, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6362.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, today the Prosecution would like to further discuss your political career. In order to be efficient with this, the Prosecution has created a chart for today's proceedings from -- containing information that the Office of the Prosecutor received from the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia about the political offices you held since 1991. Directing your attention to item 1 on the chart, does this entry correctly reflect information about your mandate as a deputy of the National Assembly between 25 January and 20 October 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not correct. I was never elected as the deputy of the National Assembly. I don't know where your information comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If that is a correction, what were you elected -- what position were you elected to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position as an MP and a deputy of the president of our group of MPs. The president of the National Assembly has his deputies. I was never one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. Did Arkan hold an office between these same dates: 25 January to 20 October 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was an MP and the president of our group of MPs, from our party.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to item 2 of this chart, does this entry correctly reflect information about your term in office between 22 January 2001 and 27 January 2004? If it does not, please feel free to make any corrections.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under item 2, if you are talking about my office as an MP, I was elected on the 23rd December, 2000. And then if you look at the second paragraph, all of that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What was your position in the Party of Serbian Unity after the assassination of Arkan on 15 January 2000?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the assassination of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, I became president of the Serbian Party of Unity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you spoke during Arkan's wedding as his best man on the 19th of February, 1995; and during his funeral you provided a eulogy on the 20th of January, 2000?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During both of these occasions, did you describe Arkan as a hero of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is still my position today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you spoke at his funeral, were you aware that Arkan had been indicted by this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the fact, as was he. But since the indictment was under seal, we were not familiar with the details of the indictment or the reasons for which he had been indicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since the indictment was under seal, how did you and Arkan learn that there was an indictment against him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the media wrote about it in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you know Arkan prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only that I didn't know him. I'd never even heard about him. I was involved in science and sports, so he wasn't someone I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence correctly, then, that you are claiming that prior to the year of 1992 you had not heard of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, in any way?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have heard certain things, but I wasn't interested in that, because the world I was living in was completely different from his world at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to item 3 on the chart, returning to it, does this information correctly reflect your term in office which -- your present term in office which began on 11 June 2008? Again, sir, if there's any corrections you would like to make, please feel free to do so. Mr. Pelevic, so you're aware, it does continue to the next page, so if you could let us know when you need that next page.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please read the remainder of that entry and let us know if that is accurate.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- if -- if this word "narodni predstavnik," "national representative," means a member of parliament, then it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Party of Serbian Unity merged into the Serbian Radical Party in December 2007?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the record, the Prosecution stated December 2007.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that the Serbian Party of Unity had difficult financial conditions, the Main Board wanted us to join either the Democratic Party of Serbia led by Kostunica or the Serbian Radical Party. Since the negotiations I was involved in with Mr. Kostunica to join the Democratic Party of Serbia didn't bear any fruit, the Main Board requested that we join the Serbian Radical Party, which is a move that I opposed. Unfortunately, I had to respect the majority decision, the decision of the Main Board, and we joined the Serbian Radical Party. As a result, everyone expect myself became a member of that party. I didn't want to become a member of that party because I didn't like the vocabulary they used, and the way in which they conducted themselves. I was in that group, as a member of parliament for a while, but I was never a member of that party. I didn't want to be a member. Tomislav Nikolic, the deputy, convinced me that things would change, that he would form another political group; and as a reason, and because of that, I remained within that party as someone who participated in the proceedings, but I wasn't actually a member.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly requested to slow down for the sake of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for that information. I do have a couple follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first again invite the witness to slow down. The interpreters have difficulties in following you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you left the association with the Serbian Radical Party on 9 September 2008 and joined a new deputy group, or MP group, called Napred Srbijo, meaning the Progressive Party?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Napred Srbija was the actual name of the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After you joined Napred Srbija, did the Defence team of Vojislav Seselj submit criminal charges to the War Crimes Prosecutor in Serbia on 4 February 2010? If you could please answer "yes" or "no" at this time, as we will further discuss these allegations from Mr. Seselj's defence shortly?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, do you mean the criminal report filed against me by the Serbian Radical Party? Is that what have you in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The criminal report that was filed against you on -- in February 2010; that's the one I'm asking you about. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders 65 ter 6362 into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6362 will receive number P3064, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At transcript page 16337, you were asked about the commander of the Territorial Defence of the SBWS, and you stated: "Yes, I know that. Because he often came to the training centre. His name was Radovan Stojicic, Badza. He was the commander of the Territorial Defence. And by virtue of that position he was our superior commander, because we were a Territorial Defence unit for the region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem." Do you recall this testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Badza attended meetings with Arkan where upcoming SDG operations were planned and co-ordinated?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Radovan Stojicic, Badza, was the TO commander, I was an ordinarily soldier, and I couldn't attend such meetings. So there's nothing I can tell you about that. I'm just repeating what I already said. He did go to the training centre of the SDG very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you aware, either through your personal observations or information you heard, as to whether Badza would arrange for the delivery of weapons and supplies to the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. Unless you have in mind deliveries from the Dalj TO that mainly consisted of ammunition, Zoljas, hand-held rocket-launchers, and grenades. In that case, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You learned of this involvement by Radovan Stojicic, Badza, after you joined the Serbian Volunteer Guard in January 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I personally saw him on a number of occasions when he went to the Guards' centre in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P1055. Page 2 of the B/C/S and page 5 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a copy of the published Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia which indicates that as of 31 December 1991 Radovan Stojicic had been officially pointed as the assistant minister of the Republic of Serbia Ministry of Interior. You were aware that Badza was the assistant minister of the Serbian MUP when you joined the SDG; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of the fact at the time, nor was I interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is a good break time. I see the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This would be. If it's a good time for you, it's a good time for a break. We'll resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At transcript page 16338, Mr. Pelevic, you were asked: "... to your knowledge, did anybody come to the training centre in Erdut while you were there, or before you were there, as a representative of the MUP of Serbia or the state security of Serbia?" Your answer: "No. I'm sure that nobody did. "There was quite a great detail of animosity between the Guards and the MUP of Serbia and especially between the Guards and the state security of Serbia. "Q. Mr. Pelevic, is it true that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, once he stopped being the commander of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja ... Western Srem, somewhat later became an assistant minister of the MUP of Serbia and the chief of the public security department?" Your answer was: "Yes. It's a notorious fact. Everybody knows that." In light of the decision we just looked at before the recess, is it correct that your previous answers are not accurate, since Badza was an assistant minister of the Serbian MUP while acting as a TO commander for the SAO SBWS?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as an ordinary soldier at the time, who'd joined the Guards on the 10th of January, that was ten days after he was appointed as a deputy minister of the interior, as an ordinary soldier I wasn't in a position to be aware of that. We didn't have any information to that effect in the Guards. And as a civilian prior to that period, I really wasn't interested in who was appointed as the -- the deputy minister. So I stand by what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain, then, while two days ago you claimed that it was a notorious fact when Badza became the assistant minister and chief of public security, and today are you diminishing your knowledge about that and saying you were not interested in it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying I was a civilian up until the 10th of January, and during that period of time I wasn't interested in that. After the 10th of January I was an ordinarily soldier, for a month or so, and I couldn't have been aware of that. Later he became the assistant of the minister of the MUP. Well, that is well-known. But at the same time I was not interested in the fact. In any event, with your leave, he never acted -- or he never went or visited as an assistant to the minister, but as a commander of the TO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We've seen that he was actually officially the assistant -- an assistant minister of the Serbian MUP. In light of that fact, are you presenting evidence saying that Arkan was actually worried about Badza stopping the Serbian Volunteer Guard at the borders between Croatia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't afraid of Badza. I will repeat what I have already said. They struck up a friendship and both of them fought together in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. And Commander Arkan was subordinated to him as a TO commander, of course. He wasn't afraid of him, but naturally he was afraid of the ordinary police that would deal with these situations in a regular manner. So these weren't affairs that had to be dealt with by the assistant to the MUP minister or by the minister himself, but he was not afraid of Badza.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you joined the Serbian Volunteer Guard, were you aware that the Serbian MUP was the institution authorised to conduct background checks in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's quite normal in all countries, including Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At transcript page 16339, you discussed the relationship between Badza and Arkan. You stated: "This was a very personal relationship, and that continued to exist all the way up to Badza's death." Is it correct that you attended Badza's funeral with Arkan in April 1997?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution would ask to play the first clip from 65 ter 6316. This clip comes from a French TV3 documentary entitled "Milosevic and his Shadow Men." A copy of this documentary with English subtitles is on the Prosecution exhibit list under 65 ter -- under 65 ter 713 with ERN V000-6775. The Prosecution is playing this version of the documentary from ERN V000-4338 because there are no subtitles. The duration of the first clip is 17 seconds. It corresponds to the 22- to 39-second segment. There is music during this video-clip, but no narration to translate. No transcript has been provided because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, did you recognise this video footage as footage from the funeral of Radovan Stojicic, Badza, on the 14th of April, 1997?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you and Arkan part of this procession that we just watched?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you see yourself and Arkan in the video-clip we just viewed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the image was very small. It was perhaps less than one quarter of the size of the screen. If the image could be enlarged to take the full screen, perhaps I would be able to assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your answer is, "No, I didn't see myself." Because that was the question. Whether it's the size of the screen or whether it's you weren't there is then the next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we appreciated that this might be a concern of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6316.1. It is a marked video still from the 36-second mark of the video-clip we just watched. And if we could please just have one copy of the -- or if we could have the still just -- single still on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I recognise myself as well as Commander Arkan. This is an entirely different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir, if I --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The still is frozen. It's a bit bigger. I recognise myself, although I can only see one part of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, so the record's clear: Is it correct that the red arrow containing the number 1 is pointing to you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the red arrow containing the number 2 is pointing to Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution tenders the still.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I hesitated to object when my learned friend tried to use this video. But I do object to its use, and I do object to its being tendered. As I understand -- or understood Your Honours' guidance on the admission of the evidence of documents tendered by the Prosecution during the Defence case, dated the 26th of August, 2011, there has to be, first of all, a good reason to use a document. That reason being to elicit evidence. And secondly, an even better reason, to actually tender a document. The witness -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me perhaps -- Mr. Weber, I think the witness said that he was present during the funeral. What's the -- is there any further purpose of --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I do have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have a further purpose. So there will be a follow-up. Then I suggest that we -- Mr. Jordash, we will first hear what the follow-up will be and then decide on admission. Because if it's just to have confirmed that he was there, which, I take it, will not be in dispute that much and which is in line with the testimony of the witness, we wouldn't need to look at it, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I'm going to show a second clip and also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- and also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see what the follow-up is. Meanwhile, we'll ask Madam Registrar to assign a number. That is, clip and still?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to use a second clip from the same 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I can tender them again together, if that's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's then -- perhaps then we leave it for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record also, the Prosecution did mention that a version of this video is already on its exhibit list; therefore, it is not fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time I would ask Mr. Laugel to please play clip 2 from 65 ter 7316. This clip comes from the same documentary. I'm going to ask Mr. Laugel to play this clip without any audio for the witness. The duration of the clip is 9 seconds and corresponds to the 1-minute, 35-second, to 1-minute, 44-second segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this as footage of Badza's funeral?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But how come that in the first part of the clip Arkan and I were in the third row, and now he is immediately after Milosevic? There were stories brought by the Serbian media --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir -- sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that this still, this image --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was falsified so as to put him right next to Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You were asked whether this is footage from the funeral.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So you reject whatever may have been said about it being a falsification or -- I would have difficulties if I see two people -- but, of course, what you could do is compare, for example, the coat of Mr. Milosevic. He was -- or the tie he was wearing that day. But, okay, your answer is, "it is," on whatever basis. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was this footage taken after the procession that we earlier watched?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. According to Serbian customs, you walk in a procession up to the grave and then you stand by the grave during the burial itself. So I suppose that the answer should be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, during your evidence here so far you've maintained that Arkan and Milosevic did not have much of a relationship, if I were to paraphrase it. In this video-clip that we just saw, it appears that Arkan is in the very immediate proximity of Slobodan Milosevic. Did you personally see Arkan and President Milosevic interact during this funeral?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no interaction at all. The fact that somebody may be seen standing next to somebody else, I don't see that as a problem. I -- and I did not see them actually talking in the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you with Arkan throughout the entire funeral?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you present at the grave-site, and did you view the grave-site ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did Jovica Stanisic play any role during these grave-site ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, did you watch any individuals in uniform fold a flag at the grave-site and see that flag provided to Mr. Stojicic's family?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular moment. But it is part of the usual custom. If a high official is buried, a folded flag is handed over to his family. I suppose that this was done by people wearing police uniforms, because I saw them in the first part of the video-clip, in the procession, next to the coffin, wearing police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders the two clips under 65 ter numbers 6316 and the still under 6316.1 as public exhibits. The reason that we're doing this is because the witness has challenged the relationship between Arkan and Milosevic and we are now offering those in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is then established by them being on the same funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In part. And not too far away from each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar informs me that the video is not in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will remedy that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll hear from you once it has been remedied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday, at transcript page 16458, you stated that the offices of the Party of Serbian Unity were located at the same address as one of the headquarters of the SDG, on Ljutice Bogdana Street in Belgrade. Did members of the SDG enlist at this location between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6353.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm calling up is an advertisement for the Serbian Volunteer Guard which was published in "Srpsko Jedinstvo," the Party of Serbian Unity publication; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How often did the Party of Serbian Unity produce its publication?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the editor-in-chief of the magazine. It was published monthly, once a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were advertisements for the Serbian Volunteer Guard included in each of these publications?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in each of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How regularly were they included?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that often. It's really very hard for me to say that after such a long time. I would say a few times. Not regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the photograph in this advertisement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know where this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you present when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not. It was taken before I joined the Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That would be in 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is the tank depicted in this photograph one of the tanks that you referred to earlier in your testimony this week?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please focus on the crest at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that this is one of the crests of the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the official crest of the SDG.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders 65 ter 6353 into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I object again on the same basis: that I can't understand the relevance, I don't understand why this is adduced by the Prosecution at this time, nor do I understand why they want to rely upon it at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So relevance is primarily the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's relevant to show the relationship between the Party of Serbian Unity producing advertisements in its own publications in the Serbian Volunteer Guard. The Prosecution submits that the objection is without merit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What's the relevance to the charges, though? I understand the relevance to Arkan, but I don't understand the relevance to the charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's relevant to -- this witness has been brought and he has offered evidence and there's been witnesses brought to discuss their relationships with Arkan and referencing the Party of Serbian Unity and what their activities were. I believe it is relevant to the credibility of this witness, first, in that there's a nexus as to what was being published in Belgrade related to the Serbian Volunteer Guard and that there was active recruitment of Serbian Volunteer Guard members through the Party of Serbian Unity in Belgrade which were then eventually sent for training. It's relevant to the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed. Then, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6353 will receive number P3065, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, you've indicated your awareness of a criminal complaint brought against you by the defence -- or by the SRS in February 2010. In relation to these allegations, did you meet with a deputy War Crimes Prosecutor and officials from the Serbian MUP on the 10th and 17th of February, 2010?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I learned from the media that I was charged with war crimes committed in Zvornik, the following day I went to see Mr. Vukcevic, who was War Crimes Prosecutor. I handed over my passport, to prove that I did not intend to leave the country, and I said that I would not convey my parliamentary immunity. And I told him that I was not in Zvornik at the time. I also attended that meeting at the War Crimes Department in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Rest assured, we're going to go through some aspects of this. If you could please focus on my questions and I will take it through -- go through it with you step by step. It is correct, then, that you met with officials from the Serbian MUP and a deputy from the War Crime Prosecutor's Office on both the 10th and the 17th of February, 2010?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not fully. The first meeting was with Mr. Vukcevic at the prosecutor's office, and the second meeting was at the War Crimes Department at the MUP of Serbia. The first meeting was not attended by anybody from the War Crimes Department of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you. On the second meeting, on the 17th of February, 2010, did you complete a written statement in which you discussed your knowledge and involvement in the Serbian Volunteer Guard between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I provided a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: A copy of your statement was provided to you after you signed each page; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You have had the opportunity over the course of almost the past two years to review this statement after it was provided to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did your statement accurately reflect what you said on the 17th of February, 2010?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to see the statement again in order to be able to answer. I don't remember the statement, to be honest, nor did I pay much attention to it, because I was completely innocent of all charges, which was eventually proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I've got no idea what is in that statement, but let's be careful here. That if the witness would answer any question and by those answers possibly incriminate himself, then he should be warned that he is not under an obligation to answer such a question unless he is ordered to do so. And the Chamber might be hesitant to give such an order, because it protects against prosecution before this Tribunal, but not necessarily for national jurisdictions. I do not know what the state of any investigation or prosecution is. But let's be -- my I invite you to be as careful as I would be if I were in your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And just so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know the statement. I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution is going to call it up. But just so the Chamber is aware: As the witness has indicated, the charges were dismissed. But we are mainly going into this for the purpose of comparing what he has said so far during his testimony and what he similarly said during the previous statement. It's not to make any overt allegation that he, in fact, committed certain crimes that he discussed in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that's the case. But I want to be very cautious in this respect. Mr. Pelevic, you may have followed the discussion. When the charges were dismissed against you, which, of course, the Chamber is not aware of, then I may take it that your statement is not really incriminating yourself, but I just wanted to verify with Mr. Weber that he doesn't put any questions to you which, if you would answer them in accordance with the truth, would tend to incriminate you. That's because you would have no obligation to answer such question. Mr. Weber will be very cautious in this respect. And you are aware of the -- your position: that you are not under an obligation to answer questions that would incriminate yourself. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6355.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, do you recognise the document that appears before you as a copy of the statement that you provided on 17 February 2010? Sir, did you receive a copy of this document? Is this the copy that you received?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the witness could see his signature -- or the signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is this your signature on the page?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is not how I sign my name. It's very similar to my signature, but I can't claim for a fact that this is my signature. My signature is a bit longer usually, and you can actually see that for yourself if you look at the document -- documents that I signed yesterday. I'm not sure that this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we go to the last page of the document. In the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, yes, that we'll zoom in on the left part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of this statement, it says: "I accept the statement that has been read to me as my own, and I am signing." After that phrase, is that your signature that appears at the bottom of the statement along with a note-taker and other individuals that were officials of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible that this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, we are now looking at a page in B/C/S and a page in English which seem not to be the same. Is it -- is the one a translation of the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is, but I do not believe that the English version has been forwarded to the last page. I believe we're still looking at the -- possibly the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but above these signatures, where we see "Borislav Pelevic," where we see "Danijela Antic," and where we see some other names, above that I see text which certainly does not appear in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the last page of the English translation. Is that better, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then what we earlier saw, is that the semi-last page?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's the semi-last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not see any signatures. Let me just have a look at this. Could I have a look at the previous page in English then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apparently what we saw before was the first page. I'm a bit confused about the several ... yes. What was on our screen a minute ago was the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could we now have a look at -- and the semi-last page, apparently there are no signatures. I now understand what caused my lacking ability to combine what I saw in B/C/S with what I saw in English. But it now is clear to me. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before we continue with this document, I'd like to ask you a question as to how you remember the precise date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have we now established that this is the signature of the witness at the bottom? I may have missed it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise -- is this -- is this the statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How do you remember the precise date of 10 January 1992 as the date you joined the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the first day after the Orthodox Christmas. It was still a bank holiday. The 7th was the Orthodox Christmas, and the holiday spilled over onto the next two days, which is why I went there on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of the B/C/S and English translation of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to the third paragraph under the word "statement," which states: "I became a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard on 10 February 1992 at the admissions HQ of the SDG in Arkan's house in Belgrade in the Ljutice Bogdana Street, so I do not have immediate information about how and in what manner the Guard participated in combat during the 1991 and in January 1992 in the Republic of Croatia in the following locations." One of those locations being Luzac. "From what the Commander Arkan and other members of the Guard said, I know that the Guard was established on 11 October 1990 in the Pokajnica monastery near Velika Plana. It participated in the territory of --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have the next page in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "... the Republic of Croatia under the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem." On Tuesday you portrayed yourself as quite knowledgeable about the SDG's early activities. At page 16336, you spoke about how the Serbian Volunteer Guard participated with the military in combat operations in 1991. In particular, you mentioned the operation at Luzac and how General Bratic and General Biorcevic commanded operations. On this same page, you go on to describe some operations that you were a part of after you joined the Guard in January 1992. If you had such information that you claim to have directly learned and experienced as a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, why did you tell the deputy War Crimes Prosecutor: "I do not have immediate information about how and in what manner the Guard participated in the combat during 1991 and January 1992 in the Republic of Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally I couldn't have had any such information, which is what I said in the course of my testimony yesterday or the day before yesterday. I quite simply knew nothing about the events from 1991. I had no direct information about those events. But given what my comrades in arms volunteers would say and what Commander Arkan and the commander of the Novi Sad Corps, General Andrija Biorcevic, had to say, I did have some indirect information, and this is what I emphasised yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. That explains the statement regarding the 1991 combat operations. How about the January 1992? You've testified now that you directly participated in operations during that time. However, this statement reflects that you said you had no immediate information about that. What is your explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could Mr. Weber please provide us with the reference. Where did the witness say that he directly participated in that operation in January? I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... well, I think the request does. Mr. Weber, could you please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I read out that on page 16336 as part of my earlier -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... one second. One second. Let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if there's any confusion, I can further clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said 16 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What I have down here is 16336.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's have a look at it. That is the 24th. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm trying to find the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So do I, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you put something to the witness, then we'd like to know where it is found, what you put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What I'm referring to is page 16336 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- starting at line 18. And through the course of the conversations, it appears that the witness is referring to a few smaller-sized operations that he participated in after he arrived in the SDG. If you would like me to, I can confirm whether or not those operations were in January 1992 to make it further clear before posing the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's any question about references, you're always invited and hereby again to put that literally to the witness and perhaps ask additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, on Tuesday you testified that you participated in a few smaller-sized operations after your arrival in Erdut. Is it correct that these operations occurred during January 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I never said that. I quite clearly said that training was obligatory for all recruits and that it was to last for three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer was -- the first "That's not correct" would have done. Yes? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When did these smaller-sized operations occur when you -- after you arrived?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that was in May or June, something like that, since first you have a three-months' training course in the Guards and then you go into action. In my statement I mentioned the operations concerned. There was one with a boat that the Romanian volunteers used within the Croatian guards. And the other one was a reconnaissance operation. That was sometime after January.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that I'm understanding that you're saying it's in -- after you came back from the Krka monastery in May or June 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct, after the return.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I again looked at your first question, which was: "How about ... January 1992? You've testified ... that you directly participated in the operation [sic] during that time." Which could not possibly be understood in any different way than January 1992. And that's not what the witness testified. So, therefore, could you please be very accurate in this respect because it creates confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not participate in any combat operations involving the Serbian Volunteer Guard prior to 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I wasn't even a member of the Guards prior to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
