utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not personally observe how members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard interacted with the Territorial Defence of the SBWS in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could testify about that and I emphasise certain things. It was only on the basis of Commander Arkan, when we became close, that I found out certain things. In 1991, there was no information I could have about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At transcript page 16322, when you were asked about how you joined the SDG, you stated: "I went to the recruiting office of the Serbian Volunteer Guard in Belgrade, I volunteered, and then two days later I was transported in a van to Erdut where the headquarters was, as well as the training centre of the Serbian Volunteer Guard." I'd like to direct your attention to the third paragraph from the bottom of the page, which states, in part: "When I showed up at the Guard HQ for the first time, I was received with suspicion, probably because I was very different to a great majority of other volunteers. Namely, I already had M.Sc. in economy by then; I was an MD of a socially-owned company, Sportinvest; and I was also the president of the Kick-Boxing Federation of Yugoslavia. I received a cold reception, and I was told that they suspected me of hiding from the law in relation to financial crimes, so they told me they had to run a check on me." What were you asked or told that made you think that they suspected you of running away from the law?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I put down in the statement is correct. That paragraph is precise. They thought that I, as the managing director of a private company, as a private businessman, that I had violated the law and that I was running from the law as a result of that. And since I had an MA and I was the only one who had an MA in the Guards, they were suspicious. They wanted to know why I who had an MA and why I who was the manager of a successful company wanted to fight for the Serbian people. They suspected me as a result of that. But later they called me. They said everything was okay. They checked things up in my company and they checked things up by contacting the general secretary of the Yugoslav Kickboxing Association.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is, once again, kindly asked to slow down for the benefit of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again ask you, perhaps if you would make shorter answers, just focussing on the question, that would also prevent achieving a speed which cannot be followed by the interpreters. So please focus very much on the questions. And you don't have to explain why your answer is the correct answer, as you often tend to do. Just give the answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were told that they thought you were hiding from the law and they were going to run a check on you, did it not cross your mind that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was going to check whether you had a criminal background with the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in that because I was quite clean and innocent. So this isn't something that crossed my mind. But I have to correct something you said, Mr. Prosecutor. They didn't say that I was running away from the law. They said that they suspected me of running from the law. There is an important distinction to be made there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How were you different from a majority of the other volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, isn't it true that the witness has answered this question. He explained to us that his level of education was by far higher and that his position in society was also at a level not ordinarily found with the others. So if you want to learn more about it, then please make a -- put a question to the witness which -- which he understands that he is not expected to repeat what he said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about how you feel that you're different from the other volunteers. So, not with respect to your own personal background, but with respect to the other volunteers. How are you distinguishing that, based on who the other volunteers are?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said in the statement, and I already repeated what I said for the benefit of the Presiding Judge, my level of education, my social position, and so on and so forth, was different in relation to that of the other volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that the other members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard included criminals?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. But I can't claim that perhaps there weren't a certain number of individuals who had previous convictions. But, as a rule, the SDG had honourable combatants who were fighting for the benefit of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was a separate organisation from the JNA with its own command structure?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My brother told me that when he returned from the battle-field where the JNA was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was a paramilitary formation that participated in joint combat operations at different times with various military formations such as the JNA, VRS, SVK, and VJ?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given what Commander Arkan and the other guards say -- said, immediately after arriving in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, the Serbian Volunteer Guards reported to the TO staff and placed themselves under the command of the TO of the region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm asking you is that, based on your experience between 1992 and 1995, did the Serbian Volunteer Guard exist as its own entity; and through agreements, did it, at different times then go and participate in combat operations with different military structures? Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDG never took independent action. As a paramilitary formation from the very beginning, it was part of the TO of the SBWS. And after the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had established, it became an integral part of that army, and as such it participated in actions with the Army of Yugoslavia and the Army of the MUP of the -- of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did your brother also join the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was previously a volunteer in the JNA. He returned home after the 45-day period had expired. That was the period during which it was necessary to be a volunteer in the JNA. He told me bad things about their command structure. After that event, he never became engaged in the military again, so he was never a volunteer in the SDG.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for interrupting. If I'm not mistaken, I think that at line 22 there was a misinterpretation. Towards the end it seems that there is just one structure that is concerned. Or, rather, it seems that there are two structures that are concerned; but, in fact, three structures are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, you -- part of your last answer was that after the SDG had become a - something - integral part of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, "and as such it participated in action with ..." And could you then repeat what you said? I think the first entity you mentioned is the Army of Yugoslavia. And then the second and possibly the third you refer to were what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of Republika Srpska and the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the next paragraph, I believe it's the second paragraph from the bottom of the page, which states: "After they completed a background check on me, they told me I was clean on 10 February 1992 and I was dispatched to the Erdut training centre for training. The Guard HQ and seat were located there." Is it correct that you reported to the location in Belgrade at Ljutice Bogdana Street before going to Erdut?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Regardless of whether it is in January or February, when within the two-day period that you've indicated were you informed that this check was completed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the following day. As early as that. I'm not sure. Perhaps a day or two later. But that was 20 years ago, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, in light of the fact that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, had been appointed officially as an assistant minister of the Serbian MUP and it took a day to do a background check, do you maintain that the SDG had no involvement with the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Given what my officials said, I know that checkups were made in my company to see whether the company was making losses, checkups were made in the kick-box association of Yugoslavia to see whether I had embezzled money, or something like that. The responses were quite decisive, and I think that was quite sufficient for the HQ in Belgrade to call me and inform me of the fact that they found that I was clean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So you're presenting evidence that the SDG did not look into your criminal background by asking with the Serbian MUP. Is that what we're supposed to understand from this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had a criminal file, a criminal record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm not saying whether you did. But in terms of their verification --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get things straight. You told us, Mr. Pelevic, that a check on your background was done. Do you know how exactly that was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said, I have information according to which they went to my office to see my secretary and the financial director and they tried to see what the situation of the company was. They also checked -- or, rather, made checks in the Yugoslav kick-box association, kickboxing association, whose president I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, would you exclude for the possibility that they would have contacted the MUP and say, "Is Mr. Pelevic known with a criminal record?" Or ... would you exclude for that possibility? Do you know whether it happened? Do you know that it did not happen? What's your position in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't exclude that possibility, but I have no information to that effect. I don't know how checks are made, because I've never had a criminal record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At transcript pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Would we be able to have a break, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it's approximately time for a break. We'll have a break. And we resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Pelevic. At transcript pages 16322 and 16324, you refer to a sergeant who you shared a room with once you arrived in Erdut. Could you please tell us his name and nickname?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would gladly, but I don't remember. I remember him telling me that he had previously worked as a waiter in a Belgrade's café-bar. He left the SDG soon thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Approximately how long were you his room-mate?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole of the three days while I was cleaning the barracks' perimeter from cigarette butts and the rest of the garbage. After that I was transferred to the dorm and joined the rest of the troops there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Today you discussed Ilija Kojic and made references to relationship of his with the Serbian DB. How did you come by this information?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Commander Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And what did Arkan tell you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details of that conversation. I did not see much of Ilija Kojic later. He was not important for the SDG at the time, although he was effectively our superior. However, we didn't have much to do with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When Arkan was -- and you were discussing Ilija Kojic, do you recall at all what he said about the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that they were our opponents; that they were trying to expel us from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem; that Ilija Kojic worked for them; and that both Milovanovic, Mrgud, and President Goran Hadzic were against Ilija Kojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that this conversation occurred in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when. Perhaps in late 1992 or perhaps early 1993. I really can't remember; therefore, I can't give a precise answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please return to 65 ter 6355 which we see may already be up. Page 3 in the B/C/S and page 4 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to the top paragraph on this page of your statement from 17 February 2010, which states: "At that time, SDG had 400 members. And from the establishment point of view, it was a reinforced battalion in strength. It had three companies in its composition and they were further split into platoons, but I don't remember how many platoons were in each company. Each company was commanded by the company commander," in B/C/S 'komandir,' "ranked as a lieutenant in the Guard and platoons were commanded by sergeants. I don't remember now the names of the company commanders, but I remember their nicknames, as that is how we addressed each other. We called the commander of my company, the 2nd Company, Zemunac. He was from Zemun and was a keen boat or kayak rower. Zika was the commander of the 1st company, and I know that he got killed in Zvornik. The commander of the 3rd Company was Ivan Okiljevic, aka Rambo, who also got killed in Zvornik. Please note that Zemunac was the commander until my departure to the Krka monastery, but by the time I returned from that position he had left the Guard. After him, the commander of my company was Milorad Ulemek, aka Legija, who I found in that position on my return from the Krka monastery. I heard that he had deflected [sic] from the Foreign Legion and joined the Guard in Zvornik." First, is this statement accurate as to the structure of the Serbian Volunteer Guard in the spring of 1992, between January and May?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Establishment-wise, there were three companies which were split into platoons. So, yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person you are referring to as Zemunac?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember his first name, Srdjan. However, yes. You asked me it tell you his name. Should we perhaps go into private session for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is -- is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, if the witness is more comfortable with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ... In itself, if you mention a name, there's no need to go into private session unless there's any specific reason for that. If you consider that it would have a certain affect on this man, then we could consider that. But the mere fact that you're mentioning a name doesn't justify to go into private session. Do you prefer to go in private session? Then please give the reasons. You could do that even in private session. Or do you say, "No, we can continue in public session"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not aware of the procedure. That's why I asked. There's no need to go into private session. His name is Srdjan Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What is the full name of the person with the nickname Zika who died in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called him Major Zika. I know that he was a taxi driver as a civilian. He worked in Belgrade. His family name was Zivanovic. I don't know what his first name was, whether it was, indeed, Zika or something else. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is the person that you're referring to as Rambo, Ivan Okiljevic, a different Rambo than Nenad Bujosevic who was known as Veliki Rambo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This one was the first Rambo. The other one was Veliki Rambo. There was a third Rambo. The third Rambo, as we called him, or Little Rambo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that third Rambo was nicknamed Mali Rambo, and do you know his name?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name. I know that he was short; hence little or Mali Rambo. He had a good sense of humour. He was a very popular volunteer. He used to entertain us with his jokes. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Marko Pejic also went to Bijeljina and Zvornik in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Bijeljina. I know that he was in Zvornik, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: After April 1992, did you continue to remain subordinate to Legija during your time in the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Establishment-wise, yes. But for a short time. Later on I was a very independent training instructor in the Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You just said: "But for a short time." What time-period are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A month, perhaps two months. Not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could I seek clarification of one of the answers. You were asked whether the person you were referring to as Rambo, Ivan, was a different Rambo than Nenad, and then a name follows. And then your answer is: "No. This one is [sic] the first Rambo." Now, apparently, in the statement we read a person by the first name Ivan, and Mr. Weber says, Is this the same as Nenad. Did he have two first names? Or what explains the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was actually trying to clarify that there are different Rambos that are referred to in the Serbian Volunteer Guard, saying that the one referred to here is not the same as Nenad Bujosevic, known as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe it's on page 57, lines 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see. The question was: "Is the person that you're referring to as Rambo, Ivan ... a different Rambo than Nenad ...?" And the answer was: "No. This one was the first Rambo." And for us then to understand that it was a different person is not obvious. I do advise you to not only put the questions but also to listen careful to the answers and see to what extent they can create confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is the person that you're referring to in your statement, Ivan Okiljevic a different Rambo, a different person, than the person who is later known as Veliki Rambo, that other person being Nenad Bujosevic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we're talking about two completely different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And we've discussed a third person that was known as Mali Rambo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you subordinate to Legija in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not subordinated to Legija.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gladly. After I was wounded, I was no longer fit for military service. I was wounded in the shoulder as well as in my left leg. Those were both serious wounds. So I could no longer serve under anybody's command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please go to the lower portion of the statement that's up on the screen in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, I'm directing your attention to the paragraph in which you state: "I arrived in the monastery on 29 March 1992 and stayed there till 25 April 1992 when I returned to Belgrade since my wife had given birth. I was granted five days' leave, after which I returned to Erdut and was awarded a rank of 2nd Lieutenant for the well-executed task in the Krka monastery." Does this statement accurately reflect the dates in which you were away at the Krka monastery and then went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose that the dates are correct. Because I was supposed to prepare for that meeting about that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you provided materials in support of your statement concerning your whereabouts in April 1992 to the War Crime Prosecutor's Office in Serbia? These materials you provided included four letters from your wife that was sent to the monastery; three photographs of you at the monastery; and a book with an inscription from the priest at the monastery, dated 10 April 1992. Did you provide those materials in support of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Weber. I was informed, Mr. Pelevic, that are you in this courtroom in possession of a mobile phone and that you are using it in whatever way through SMS or that you are ... Could I invite you to switch it off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it has been switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, earlier it was reported to me that you took it out of your pocket and that you -- well, used it in whatever way. Could I -- Yes, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I observed from here. And what happened is that his phone went off and he reached into his pocket and turned it off. That's how I saw it from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then that has been now clarified to me. It happened to me once in the last ten years that my phone went off in this the courtroom, Mr. Pelevic. So it is, although rare, it does happen now and then, and I'm glad that you switched it off. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All of these materials concerning your whereabouts in April 1992 were returned to you after you provided your statement in February 2010; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so. But I can't remember, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you ever provide any of these materials to the Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. They never asked me to do that. Nobody ever asked for those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you in possession of those materials here in The Hague this week?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that they would be required, that I was supposed to bring them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that during your interview on the 17th of February, 2010, you were provided with a copy of the criminal complaint that was submitted by the Defence of Vojislav Seselj?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I have ever seen that criminal complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During the course of your interviews, did you learn the identity of any protected witness who may have been referred in a criminal complaint? If you did, could you please not say the name of the witness, if you learned this information.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I learned about three different individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, would you like to go into private session for this purpose? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I do not plan to actually use the name of the witness and was going to stay in open session. However, I did want to learn if the witness knew the identity of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So please refrain from mentioning any name. You didn't do that, so you were cautious as well. You may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you learn that this witness never actually identified you, as stated in the allegations that were brought by the Seselj Defence team?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Prosecutor Vukcevic told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For cross-reference for the Chamber, the Prosecution would refer to Exhibit P113.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, during this interview you were also shown some photographs which were marked, I believe, during your interview as numbers 1 through 7; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P117; e-court page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, is it correct that you made the following observations of this photograph, and I quote from your February 2010 statement: "A member of the Guard whom we called Suca and who got killed is in the forefront of the photograph marked number 5 where he is holding a green flag in his right hand. I cannot recognise the three men with Balaclavas and I cannot recognise the person on the outmost right of the photograph, although his face is visible, as there were around 500 combatants at that time and I did not have to remember them all, particularly because some 10.000 combatants went through the Guard during the times of the war." Does this statement accurately reflect what you said about this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In your comments to the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor's Office, you said "... were around 500 combatants at that time," in reference to this photograph. What time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the photo was taken. I suppose that it was taken in the Republika Srpska because I recognise the flag that belonged to the Muslim forces. I really don't know when or where the photo was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were previously shown this photo, you identified Suca. Is it correct that the full name of this person is Nebojsa Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What type of weapon is Suca holding?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photo is rather dark. It's very hard for me to discern the weapon. I believe that he is carrying what I believe is an automatic rifle in his left hand. But I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Suca is wearing a Motorola on his vest which was used by members of the SDG to communicate during combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see a Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were these Motorolas used by the SDG to communicate during combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers and junior officers did use such devices, but not all soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How would the officers and junior officers use these devices during combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had codes, and we would call each other up by using those codes if we wanted to contact a certain officer or junior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. How would these codes be provided to the officers and junior officers?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the code "Tiger 22." Usually it would be based on the date of birth of the officer or junior officer in question. That would be his code. If someone was born on the 15th of any month, then that person's code would be Tigers 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the code "99" was assigned to Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He used that code throughout the war-time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And when you say "throughout the war-time-period," are you saying that you have direct knowledge of that between 1992 and 1995? For example, did you ever use Motorolas to personally contact him by using the code "99"?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end of that year. The end of 1992. We addressed him as "Commander," as a rule. But sometimes, for conspiratorial reasons, we called him "99," which was his war-time code.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Suca was killed after the war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have e-court page 8 of this same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, did you provide these following comments to the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor about this photograph: "Commander Arkan is in the middle of the photograph number 6. To the left of him, on his right side, is the above-mentioned Suca. And to the right of him, i.e., on his left side, is a person who bent his head and has a beret which prevents me from recognizing his face. I also do not recognise the other people on this photograph whose faces are only partially visible." Does that accurately describe your statement on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know when this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know where this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You can't see any indications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: A question not related to the photograph: Is it correct that Suca participated in the Velika Kladusa operations at the end of 1994 and beginning of 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't answer that question. I don't know. Perhaps he did; perhaps he didn't. I can't speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In the comments I have read to you about the earlier photograph, you stated that: "... some 10.000 combatants went through the Guard during the times of war." Who are the 10.000 people that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim that there were 10.000 people exactly, but there was several thousand men who went through the Guards and were trained. They first had a one-month period there, and then three-month periods. The composition of the men kept changing. Some would come, some would leave. So it was very difficult to assess how many volunteers there were in the centre, how many had been trained, how many had left. But throughout that period of time, my assessment would be that there were about 10.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're referring to throughout a period of time. Is that between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have the entire war-time-period in mind. There were a lot of volunteers who would join up in Republika Srpska, for example. So the number was constantly changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were all these people a part of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, or were there individuals who came from other units or military structures that were also trained there? For example, like, SVK army members or VRS or VJ members.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were men from the SVK. I know that because some SVK troops joined my company when we went to Benkovac in January --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter heard the year 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please repeat the year. Benkovac in January of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would the training that would be provided to these men from the SVK, or individuals from the SVK, was it the same training that you yourself received as a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the same form of training, since, at the time, they already had some military experience. So they didn't require physical training, just the basics of war strategy and -- and warfare. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When the individuals from the SVK came to the training, were members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard able to discipline and impose penalties upon them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While they were part of the SDG, they had to abide by SDG rules. But we're dealing with a very brief period of time and with a very small number of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that these individuals, after being trained by the SDG, would return to the units that they had been a part of?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three-month contracts weren't signed with them so they could freely return to their units, having completed the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could I seek clarification of one of the answers. You said: "... very brief period of time." How long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About a week. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "A very small number of men." How long -- how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our unit left with about 500 men to the Benkovac battle-field towards the end of January 1993. I assume that there was about -- a company from the SVK that had been attached to us in order to bring our men up to strength. So I would say that there weren't more than a hundred men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, then, therefore, that only a hundred men during approximately one week were trained in the centre, which were, to say so, outsiders and not from the SDG, and all others trained there were SDG members. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6351.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a video still of a photograph that was broadcast on B92. Do you recognise this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you appear in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to go through with you in a second who everyone is in this photograph. But if could you please tell us, first, When and where was this photo taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph was taken in Erdut. I don't know the year. Perhaps in 1994. Something like that. But this photograph was taken in a studio. It was taken for our calendar. You can see in the background that we have some sort of cloth that is usually used when photographs are taken in studios.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Starting with the top row, could you please identify the individual on the left and then the individual on the right.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the left, you can see Major Dimitrije Jasek, also know as Mita, who was killed in Velika Kladusa. To the right, you can see Milorad Lukovic, Legija. Below him, to the right, you can see Commander Arkan. And to the left, you can see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It appears that you are holding a shotgun in this photo. Was this the type of weapons that the SDG would use in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Shotguns are used for hunting. They weren't used in combat operations. This is something I had just for the photograph. I always had an M-70 automatic rifle on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us the type of weapon that Arkan is holding and whether or not that was used by the SDG in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is holding a small automatic Heckler rifle. It's made by Heckler & Koch. As I have already said, I said that yesterday or the day before, only some officers used such weapons. But I said it wasn't a combat weapon. It's a weapon that is used more for urban combat, not in the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What type of weapon is Legija holding in the upper right corner; and did the SDG use those type of weapons?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a carbine. It's also a hunting weapon. We never used that sort of weapon either. It's not an appropriate weapon for the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Lastly, with respect to Mita in the upper left, what type of weapon is he holding; and did the SDG use that type of weapon in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see it quite clearly, but I think it's a machine-gun, a light machine-gun; and such weapons were used in military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It appears that on Arkan's right sleeve that a patch is visible. Are you able to recognise this as the Tiger patch of the Serbian Volunteer Guard? Please let us know if you need us to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I can see the Tiger patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It does not appear from this photo that any other patches are visible. Is it correct that the Serbian Volunteer Guard would not always wear patches related to the Krajina military?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the sleeves of the combatants here, I can't even see the insignia, the patches. I can't see what Arkan has on his right-hand side. As far as I can see, I don't have anything on my left arm. But I don't know when the photograph was taken, as I said. It's not that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in a second. The members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard who wore uniforms, did they have velcro on their sleeves which allowed patches to be attached and removed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the whole, yes. But, unfortunately, from the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, we didn't receive any patches that could be simply put on the velcro. The patches we received had to be sewn on. There were two such patches. Patches for officers did have velcro. But for the troops, for the army, you had to sew them in, sew them on. They were green. But officers had blue patches, as far as I can remember. I think that was the situation. It said, or the inscription read: The Serbian Army of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly that you had, then, separate uniforms, uniforms that had the Krajina patch permanently sewn on and then different uniforms that had velcro that could attach and remove patches? Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders the exhibit, 65 ter 6351.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6351 will receive number P3066, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During your testimony there's been a discussion of a large convoy, which you've also mentioned just a moment ago, of SDG personnel who deployed to the western part of the RSK in early 1993. Is it correct that this large convoy of SDG personnel, in which you personally deployed, was the only time that you participated in a convoy as a member of the SDG? I guess the easier way of asking that was: Aside from the convoy in early 1993, did you participate in any other large convoys of SDG members?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, let me correct you. I didn't dispatch that convoy. I was in that convoy. It was the only convoy with which I travelled amongst so many men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. That is what I meant to refer to. So it's clear: As a SDG member, the only convoy which you travelled in was the one in early 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P2616.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, this is a SVK Main Staff security and intelligence report dated 20 February 1993. I'd like to direct your attention to the paragraph of the report that says: "Zeljko Raznjatovic, aka Arkan, commands his units, allegedly pays 5.000 DM, and they are not interested in defending the territory but in taking control of Zadar in order to loot the local banks' gold and foreign currency." Is it correct that members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard were paid 5.000 Deutschemark during your deployment to the western part of the Krajina in early 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says 5.000 German marks here, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Were you paid that amount in the spring of 1993 during these -- during your operations, your deployment?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We weren't paid a cent. This is a lie spread by the secret Army of Vojna Krajina. Who could have given 500 soldiers 5.000 German marks a month?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, sir, isn't this the army that you claim to be a part of?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the army's secret service. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Wouldn't the army's secret service of the army that you claim to be a part of know about your activities?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this information should be checked. And the security administration of the Main Staff should be informed, as far as I can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know why they were sending it to the VJ, this information? If you could please read on in the report.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact that every army has its security service. These services are always in conflict [Realtime transcript read in error "contact"] with the MUP security service or with certain units, such as the SDG. These things here -- it's a matter of laying an ambush for the SDG, because who could have 500 soldiers and pay each one 5.000 marks? I think these security services do this. It's common practice. They're always in conflict [Realtime transcript read in error "contact"] with each other. And that was the case in the Army of Yugoslavia and in the Army of Republika Srpska and in the Serbian state security. They're always against us because we were always in their way. It also mentions taking control of Zadar. That was never the objective of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina or of the SDG. As part of that army, why would we take Zadar? We just wanted to liberate Maslenica, that had been taken by the Croatian forces which committed war crimes in flagrant violation of the agreement that had been reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to what you just said, you say with respect to the security services that they're always in contact with each other. How did you know that the security services communicated or were in contact with one another?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because General Andrija Biorcevic continued to warn the commander and myself, and he told us to watch out for the security services, the army's security service and the police's security service. He told us to be wary of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I try to understand one of your last question: "Do you know why they were sending it to the VJ, this information?" Now, I see the document, apparently one -- the Main Staff of the RSK sending information to others which they say they have received from the Security Administration of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Now, who exactly did you mean by "they"? Is that those who provided the information to the security administration of the Army of the Federal Republic? Is that ... It was just --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a bit unclear who you refer to. And I don't know whether the witness was perhaps not very -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be permitted, I will try to clarify. And thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, the document before you, in one of the final paragraphs, says: "This information," reflecting the information in this report, "is forwarded to you so that you should check the data and take measures to prevent the above-mentioned deviant behaviour." There's then a request: "Please forward the information to the UB of the GS," General Staff, "of the VJ," Yugoslav Army. Do you know whether the security and intelligence administration of the RSK, why they would be forwarding or submit a request to forward information to the General Staff of the VJ, security administration?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could we very carefully look at it. Who is saying what, Mr. Weber? The document starts by saying: "We have received the following information from the security administration." And then there follows a text, which is in quotation marks. Now, if you were asking why the intelligence of the administration of the RSK would do what is -- what you read --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what we see is that the request is the request as quoted, apparently coming from the security administration of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army. So, therefore, your question seems, unless I've misunderstood the document, seems not to reflect what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Mr. Bakrac, that was the matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is exactly what I wanted to raise. And then you did it -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, perhaps I should have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- instead of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... allowed you to do it first. But it was a question that was prominently on my mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know how security administrations from the military would communicate with intelligence services of the Serbian MUP, whether they did; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this does not arise from this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has been taken out of a different context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not hear in the question put by Mr. Weber that this relates to this document. It is a general question, but perhaps it would have been wiser to inform the witness that this question is unrelated to what we find in the document. Could you please repeat the question, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document that does not relate -- this is a question that does not relate to the document: Do you know how security administrations from the military would communicate with intelligence services such as the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you waiting for my answer? Or was this an answer to the Presiding Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Weber has asked you, has repeated his question, whether you know how security administrations from the military would communicate with intelligence services such as the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Weber, how should I know that? How should I be in a position to answer questions about the practices of the security administrations, of the military, or the intelligence services of the Serbian MUP? None of us in the Guard were familiar with the methodology of the work of either the secret services of the army or the police. We never reacted to this type of letters. This -- those were all entrapments set up in order to compromise the SDG, an organisation that was in everybody's way at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, it's fine if you just let us know if you know or don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6354.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I, nevertheless, could I ask one question in relation to your last answer, Mr. Pelevic. You say this is all comprising the SDG. Let's look, for example, at one line saying that the -- let me just check. No, could I -- I see there's now another document on the screen. I would like to have the previous one back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was Exhibit P2616.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Yes, it's ... reading this, my first question would be -- the volunteers of the SRS, the Serbian Radical Party detachment, Dragi Lazarevic. That's where it starts with. And later it refers to Zeljko Raznjatovic, also known as Arkan, who commands his unit. And then there's information about that unit. Are the two -- are these two totally separate units, or did they operate together, the Dragi Lazarevic and the units of Arkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two completely different units, these are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any possibility for you to verify to what extent the other information is accurate, that is, about the Dragi Lazarevic Detachment? Do you have any information which would allow you to say that this is accurate information or wrong information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was a Serbian Radical Party unit. They were the so-called Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We heard from people when we were there that their behaviour was not very good, and people complained about them. I don't know whether they were under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska, but in any case, we didn't fight together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the information you heard about that unit was that they behaved badly. So in that respect, at least, the report is in accordance with the information you received about that unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I can see from this report, most of the letter is about that unit. Two paragraphs are about them; one about us. But it is impossible that they wanted to launch an attack on Zadar. What was in nobody's plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, yes, that was not my question. My question was whether the other part not related to Arkan's units, whether that information would be in accordance with the information you had received, although informally and not a kind of a formal report. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, due to the time, I'm just going to try and finish off on the questions about the statement that we've been using. Could the Prosecution please return to 65 ter 6355. Bottom of page 3 in the B/C/s and bottom of page 5 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we're going to be returning to your statement from February 2010, and I'd like to direct your attention to the last sentence on the page that will be appearing before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have page 3 in the B/C/S. I see that the correct page in the English is before us. And if we could have the bottom of the page of both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to the sentence that talks about the consequence of your wounding in 1993. You state: "Due to this wound, I was assessed as 80 per cent disabled and I never took part in any more combat activities." Who assessed you as 80 per cent disabled?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A medical military board did that. At the Medical Military Academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you receive any --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the hospital called the Medical Military Academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you receive any disability pay in relation to this injury?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. Because the state of Serbia does not recognise the time that we spent on the front line. Only the authorities of Republika Srpska recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please continue to the next page, top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, was it your intention to limit the question, as the witness did in his answer? He said Republika Srpska authorities do recognise it. I do not know whether you're interested to know whether the witness receives a disability pay from the Republic of Serbia or, more generally, from whomever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was going to ask some further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Since we are here:

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you receive disability pay from anyone? From the Republika Srpska or anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. Velebit was never in Republika Srpska. It's a mountain in Croatia, so, if anything, I would have to apply for that from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I'm looking at the clock. It's a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I get your time estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have another full session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One more full session. How much time, Mr. Bakrac, do you think you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the time being, I believe that I will need no more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The same. Or could I have 15 actually, please. Only because there's one issue that I forgot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You get 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first session will be 75 minutes, Mr. Weber. After that, we are not limited to 75 minutes. But for the first session we are. Not because of Mr. Stanisic, but for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. If I could get a full 75 minutes, I'd appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 75 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic will not return, for the reasons I indicated earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And he has -- it's on the record that he waived his right to be present this afternoon. We take a break. And we resume at quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At this time the Prosecution would like to tender the statement that we've been referring to, 65 ter 6355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I inquire as to whether that's being tendered for the truth of its contents or for impeachment purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the portions that have been verified by the Prosecution with the witness, for the truth of its contents. And then also obviously as to any variation that's been discussed with respect to statements in court and statements that are contained in the statement, we'd be reserving our right to make later submissions on the credibility of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection from either Defence team. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6355 will receive number P3067, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 6354.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, what's going to be called up before you is a article that was published in "Vecernje Novosti" on the 4th of October, 1995. I would like to ask about some statements of yours that are contained in this article. In the B/C/S, this is located on the lower left window of the newspaper article. And it is in the middle of the English version. Sir, I'd like to direct your attention to the section that states: "Pelevic stressed the importance of the Guard, which, as he said, prevented the fall of Sanski Most and participated in the defence of Novi Grad. He did not deny that deserters had their heads shaved and are then returned to their units." Then there's a direct quote of yours, according to this article: "'On the territory of the Serb Republic, we formed three centres for the reception of deserters,' Pelevic confirmed. 'We send them back to their units; although we are aware that they will never be soldiers, however, they can at least help others. In accordance with the old Serbian custom, the deserters who were unit commanders also had their heads shaved, are given 25 lashes, and tied to the pillar of shame.' "Although such behaviour resulted in disputes with some generals, which have all been overcome, 'a firm military hand prevented the fall of Sanski Most and Novi Grad (Bosanski Novi),' according to Pelevic. Apart from that, as Pelevic said, the guardsman also beat up a colonel of the Serb Republic Army who ordered a withdrawal from Sanski Most, and he was added to the list of officers who will answer for cowardice on the front. Pelevic could not say how many names were on this list, however, he confirmed that these men would definitely be tried, 'if this has not been done already, immediately and militarily on the front.'" Sir with respect to your direct quotations in this article, are they accurate? Are these things that you said?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a newspaper article. As much as I can see, this is a report from a press conference that I have held in Belgrade. Journalists have a tendency to make attractive articles with catching headlines. What is, though, true is that in Republika Srpska, in the region of Banija in 1995, we indeed had a problem with deserters. If we came as volunteers from Serbia via the Republic of Krajina, went there to defend their homes, it was not fair for them to desert, and that is why they were punished. Concerning the issue of shaving their heads, I myself had my head shaved when I was on Mount Velebit because that's a good hygiene measure. A soldier on the front cannot wash his hair every day. So this was not any special form of punishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would just like to go through your comments. According to this article, you stated: "On the territory of the Serb republic we formed three centres for the reception of deserters." Did you say that; and is that accurate? A simple "yes" or "no" is fine.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't have any sort of centres for the reception of deserters. This is an interpretation that was made by the journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So you are now denying today that you made that direct quote. Do I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, from the ministry of police of Republika Srpska Tomislav Kovac, we received an order to become involved in sending deserters back to their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question. I just simply asked you: Do I understand correctly that today you are denying making that direct quote?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the word "nijecete" means that I don't accept it, then I don't accept that I said this. This is a newspaper article and therefore cannot be a proper document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. According to this newspaper article, it continues with another quote of yours: "We send them back to their units, although we are aware that they will never be soldiers. However, they can at least help others. In accordance with the old Serbian custom, the deserters who were unit commanders also have their heads shaved, are given 25 lashes, and tied to it the pillar of shame." Did you make that statement; and is that accurate as to what happened?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not accurately reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the shaving of heads and providing 25 lashes and tying to a pillar of shame, did the Serbian Volunteer Guard apply that penalty to any of its own members?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not in the region of Banija because we didn't have the pillory there. This measure was applied to members of the Guards who were prisoners in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What time of infractions would merit this type of penalty?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, drinking alcohol. AWOL when this was not permitted. Soldiers went to town without permission. So these measures were applied in such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did your efforts in helping the Republika Srpska authorities in the area of Sanski Most help the VRS? Did it help them maintain their rank, specifically?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Who did it help maintain their ranks? I'm sorry, Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let's just go step by step. You've indicated that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was in the area of the Banja Luka region in September and October 1995, and do I correctly understand that during that time the SDG was putting forth efforts with respect to deserters from the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only briefly, pursuant to an order from the MUP minister of Republika Srpska, Tomislav Kovac. Soon thereafter, he withdrew this order and let this job be done by the police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry to interrupt to, Your Honours. I'm just wondering, as I've sat here for the last five minutes, wondering what the dispute is. I don't think it's disputed from this side of the room that this is the role Arkan's men played or this is the type of punishment he gave to his -- to men in Erdut or that he had the role of arresting deserters or that that order came from Kovac and ultimately from Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, then my question based off that would be to the witness - I don't know if he heard that - is whether or not that helped the Republika Srpska authorities at all in Sanski Most and Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Or that it helped in those places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are refining the question, Mr. -- you would say "or that it helped in those places" is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. None of that series of questions has been in dispute, and I don't think anyone from the Defence has ever disputed those things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution then would tender 6354 into evidence and will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would say, for the same reason, that there's no point putting in a statement which ultimately the witness has denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there's no dispute. And you might even, in view of the answers of the witness, you might even have difficulties there, but Mr. Jordash at least doesn't deny. But now, we have two Defence teams. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. I would like to refer the Chamber to D28, which shows when the order was issued. And the next document is 1D1607. But when time comes, with your indulgence, I'm going to clarify this issue with the witness very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Bakrac, what Mr. Jordash does is to say that the matter is not in dispute, which means that there's agreement between the parties. What you are doing at this moment, you are referring us to evidence which still has to be evaluated. And what is your position? Is there any dispute on any of the matters Mr. Jordash told us there was no dispute as far as the Stanisic Defence is concerned? How, as far as the Simatovic Defence is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no dispute. I only want to demonstrate that this situation lasted for an extremely short period of time, and I'm going to prove how it started, how long it lasted, and how it ended. So there is no dispute, but only concerning a very short period that we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if Mr. Weber would agree with that, there would be even no need to -- to establish that. Mr. Weber, however, I would, although on the content of this, I would have one or two questions for the witness which are not exclusively oriented to the truth of the content. Mr. Pelevic, you told us that shaving the heads was not punishment. And then a few questions after you gave this answer, you were asked by Mr. Weber about punishment and he there mentioned shaving heads, and you didn't say, You should exclude that because that was no punishment. So in one answer you say it's no punishment; in another answer you seem to accept that Mr. Weber presented it to you as one form of punishment. Could you please clarify your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, this is not shaving a head. This is just cutting hair very short. I can show you a photograph of mine where you can see that I am shaved, my head is shaved. And in my view this is not a form of punishment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the way in which you do your hairdressing that it is not a form of punishment. But, of course, that goes to the margins of what we're talking about: Were people shaven, their heads, as deserters, in combination with other punishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, at the time, I was not in the field, with the exception of five or six days went I went to visit the Guard. Therefore, I did not witness any punishment. I know that the soldiers from Republika Srpska were slapped in the face, the soldiers who ran away. And I think that the journalist made a confusion, a mix-up, between the two. This -- these measures of punishment were applied to the prisoners and -- in Erdut, but in no way could it have happened in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why could it not have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite simply, we didn't have a pillory. It was a front line. We didn't have a barracks there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, was shaving the heads of -- of deserters what -- was that an old custom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This is not a Serbian custom. The Serbian custom is 25 lashes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say you've never observed whether people were -- their heads were shaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But when I was there, I noticed that when we were sending back a VRS soldier, Arkan slapped a lieutenant-colonel from the VRS on the face, the one who had withdrawn his unit from the front line, and that was done in the presence of Colonel Talic -- General Talic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they all still had their grown hair, not very short or shaven completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This colonel was slapped in the face, and General Talic and the commander ordered him to send his unit back. There was no trimming of the hair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're talking about one case. I'm talking about a story of what happened to those who had deserted, and not about one case. Can you tell us anything else about others that had deserted and whether their heads were shaven, yes or no? If you don't know, fine; if you do know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. But I don't think that it was likely. I think that the journalists mixed this up with Erdut altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't want to interrupt, but there was a mistake on page 89, line 7, and therefore I would kindly ask, respectfully, the Chamber to ask that this pillory be repeated, and the 25 lashes -- could it be repeated who this punishment was applied to? Because I don't think that it was properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll check that. You told us that the "journalist made a confusion" - that's at least what you said - between what happened in the field and what happened in Erdut. And you then said: "These measures of punishment were applied to" - and that's how it was translated to us - "... to the prisoners and" - and that's not translated - and other persons in Erdut. And you then added: "But in no way could it have happened in the Republic of Serbian Krajina." Could you please repeat that answer. The measures of punishment were applied to whom exactly, in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, the prisoners who breached rules, like alcohol consumption or going AWOL.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just following on that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You're saying the "members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard and prisoners." Who were the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think -- I think I understand what you want to say, Mr. Bakrac. I think that if we first receive the answer of the witness, it might be clear anyhow. Could you please give an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I clearly said that these measures were applied in Erdut to members of the Serbian Volunteer Guards who were punished for it. I'm not talking about any prisoners or whatever. I'm only talking about SDG members who breached our rules, such as alcohol consumption or going to town without permission at a wrong time, and that is the only thing that I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time still tenders 65 ter 6354, as it does relate to the witness's credibility, and for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection? Tendered for credibility reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam, Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6354 will receive number P3068, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time I'm going to ask Mr. Laugel to please play a clip from a video compilation that was provided to the Prosecution from the Simatovic Defence. It is our understanding that that is one of the videos that was provided by Mr. Pelevic. It is from chapter one on one of the DVDs that we were provided at time-code 27 minutes, 50 seconds, to 28 minutes, 46 seconds.
