I do not know if the -- I do not -- at this time we do not have an available transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is there text spoken which you would like to be on the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there's no transcript. That creates a problem usually, depending on the speed of speech, but what to expect from the person on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just wanted to forewarn that -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now, I do understand that you received this video only recently, Mr. ... Let's see how far we come. And one thing is for certain: You will have to prepare a transcript anyhow in the near future if you want this to be admitted into evidence. And then we'll also be able to compare what we receive now as translation. And, again, it's an almost impossible task for our interpreters, I'm aware of that. However, the circumstances that Mr. Weber received the video only very recently justify that he couldn't prepare any transcript. If -- I'd like to hear, after we've played the video-clip, whether the interpreters -- to what extent they were able to follow, and also to hear any further comment on audibility or whatever it is. And if need be, to have it played for a second time, if, for example, you could cope with it for halfway and then lost track. And then to see whether it could be played twice. I fully understand that this is not the most pleasant job to do at this moment for our interpreters. It is exceptionally that we allow it to be done. Mr. Weber, another way of dealing with the matter would be that if it's -- if these are long parts with a lot of words spoken, to stop after every 10 seconds or 15 seconds then to see whether the interpreters can catch up. And I'm looking at you. I hope that perhaps the 15-seconds - rule I wouldn't say, but approach, would serve you best at the moment. Could I hear, on behalf of all the booth, from, for example the English booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will very much depend on the speed of speech that we are about to hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you prefer the 15-seconds approach to start with, in order to avoid that we end up in a total mess?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a possibility to pause after every 15 seconds?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's look at the video and hear what is said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speech was in Italian, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least I heard a lot of Italian words as well. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I've been informed by my partner that there's a upcoming B/C/S portion. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, so the first portion played, and we are now at 28 minutes 03, in chapter 3, is Italian language, not presented as evidence by the Prosecution. We'll then see what language now follows.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Europe talks about ethnic cleansing as a very ugly occurrence. What do you think of this aspect of the war? "I believe it to be a very negative occurrence. It is a great disgrace to drive away people from their hearths, regardless of whether they are Croats, Muslims, or Serbs. "As the Serbian Volunteer Guard and as a party, we were strictly opposed to ethnic cleansing at all times. We believe that people need to be enabled to live in their native areas. It is their right. We were in favour of this approach, but the other side did not honour that. "Admittedly there were such cases on the Serbian side as well, but we've always condemned them and we believe them not to be good." Can the footage be repeated. We couldn't hear the last part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the last part be repeated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It was only the part where the lady started speaking, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution does not intend to rely on -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To rely on --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At what the lady was saying. Then, under those circumstances, I think we'd proceed. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this quote, you appear to indicate that there were cases on the Serbian side and that you've always condemned them. Could you please explain what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant at the time and what I still mean by that is that everything needs to be resolved through peaceful means. What I had in mind in this particular footage was -- footage were specific cases, and I mean the war crimes committed by soldiers on the Serbian side against the Muslims and Croats. It was with these issues in mind that I felt a great sympathy with the victims and those who suffered from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what the SDG policy was in terms of consequences to any SDG members who carried out any such acts of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have not had such instances in the Serb Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday we viewed a part of your speech from the five-year anniversary of the Serbian Volunteer Guard in 1995. In this speech, you state: "All those who have been accused of something are amnestied." What type of crimes were you amnestying in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that they were war crimes. I said that all the prisoners of the Serbian Volunteer Guard were amnestied. And they were -- most of them were individuals who were dismissed from the Serbian Volunteer Guard for various breaches, but we amnestied only those who expressed contrition and who, through their activities, proved that they would in the future abide by the rules of the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What are the various breaches that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me give you a few examples. Insubordination; a failure to abide by the orders from superiors; frequent consumption of alcohol; going AWOL to a neighbouring town. In one instance, a guardsman was punished for having taken 200 German marks from one of the officers on the boat, or ship, that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, in the videos that we were provided, it was clear that we were watching portions of your speech and that portions were missing. We also, in this interview, noticed that you were asked a question by a journalist about allegations of ethnic cleansing in Sanski Most, and your answer was then cut at the end. Do you have a complete version of both your speech and also this interview that we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I handed the video footage to the Defence and they, in turn, handed it over to you. I don't think that anything was cut out. In the interview, I condemned ethnic cleansing, whoever may have committed it, be it the Serbs, Muslims, or Croats. I said that the SDG and the party were strictly opposed to ethnic cleansing because it was a sin and disgrace to chase away anyone from their hearths, from the areas where their fathers and forefathers were born. And I was quite clear on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you stated: "I collected everything that concerned the commander, in digital form or in printed form. I have a lot of such material." With respect to the DVDs that you provided to the Defence, did you create these DVDs from different clips, or copied the videos from other digital material?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mika Aleksic, a film and theatre director from Belgrade, who handed over that footage to me. He could be seen on that day, on the 10th of October, 1995, when the Guard had its celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you possess the raw or original video footage that you were provided in relation to your speech from 1995 in this video interview?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. Whatever I had I handed over to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What format did Mika Aleksic give you the videos in, according to you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were CDs or DVDs back then. I think it was a VHS tape, or a Beta. I'm not really sure about it. But it was a cassette, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you still have this VHS or Beta tape?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I copied it. Or, rather, it was my neighbour, who owns a video club, suggested that I have it copied to a more modern sound -- or image record. That was the DVD. And I still have those cassettes back at home. If you want me to, I can bring them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you copied it to digital format, how did you make the decisions of what to copy?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't make that decision. There was no selection involved. There was no cutting or editing. What you see on the cassettes is what you get on the CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you provide the original VHS or Beta tape to the Simatovic Defence?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Pelevic has just said that he kept the cassettes back at home, that he had them copied. I don't see why Mr. Weber should doubt that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, he said that he had them at home at this moment. He didn't say that he never had given them. And, again, the same -- the same came to my mind. The question is not exactly the same, and that's the reason why I have not intervened. At the same time, of course, we can ask ourselves where this all leads to. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would you be willing to provide those original tapes to the Simatovic Defence so the Prosecution could also view them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also is wrong, Mr. Weber. Because they were never provided to the Simatovic Defence. So to say is that the Prosecution also look at them is a wrong understanding of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What I'm asking, you, sir, is that in the future, after your testimony, are you willing to provide those videotapes so we could look at them, the original footage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, are you willing to do that? Apparently the Prosecution wants to verify whether what is on the original VHS or Beta tapes, whether that actually - and you told us you didn't do it yourself - actually everything appears on the DVDs you have provided. Are you willing to make that available? Not to say that it would not be returned to you, most likely, or at least a copy be returned to you, so you will not lose it forever. Are you willing to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be willing to give all the tapes I have that are of no use to me anymore, since I don't have a VCR at home, to Their Honours, the Prosecution, or the Defence. I am willing to give all the original tapes about the history of the Guard. There are three original films out of which I produced two documentaries about the Guard, and I am prepared to give all of that to you, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, through Victim and Witness Section, I take it that a means will be found how to make that available, also to make further arrangements on copying or returning originals to you, or copies to you. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yesterday when you were shown a certificate for an individual named Aleksandar Drazovic, you stated: "It is one of ... many regular documents." What type of documents do you have in any files relating to individuals who are member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Arkan's death, I took from his desk, from his office, everything that had to do with the Guard. In the main, these were lists of the wounded and the families of those who had been killed and who were now receiving permanent assistance. And I handed all these documents over to Mr. Vukcevic at the request of the prosecution in Belgrade. There were two cardboard boxes. That was all. What happened with the archives of the Guard once it was disbanded, I don't know. We never kept these records, although I do have at home a large frame containing the photographs of all of our soldiers who were killed. There were 50 of them. Beneath every photograph there's the first and last name, date of birth, date and place of death. And there is no problem at all. I can make arrangements for ICTY representatives to have a look at that at my home immediately. There would be no problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you say you provided the documents to Mr. Vukcevic, you're saying that they were provided to the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor's Office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Vukcevic. Is that correct, that that's then what you provided to the Serbian War Crimes Office?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who did you provide the documents to? When you say you provided them to Mr. Vukcevic, who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed it over to the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor's Office, namely to the prosecutor in chief, to the chief prosecutor of that office, Mr. Vukcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were included on the Simatovic Defence witness list on 6 June 2011. The Simatovic Defence included some of the documents that you provided to them on their exhibit list which was filed on that same date. My question to you is: When were you first contacted to be a witness in this case prior to June 2011, if you were?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know when it was, but I know the name of the lawyer, Zoran Jovanovic, from the same office. Unfortunately he died in the meantime. He was the first one to get in touch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that you were contacted sometime prior to the fall of 2009?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Truly, I don't know. It could have been back then, but I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 2D904, page 1 of both the B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is there a document before you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is this a statement you provided or submitted to the military records section in Banja Luka of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska dated 4 May 2011?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you sent this statement after you were contacted to be a Defence witness at a later point in time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you sent this statement at a point in time which was after you had been contacted to be a Defence witness in this case?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. But I don't see the connection. This is part of my regular duties that I do at the request of our veterans who were wounded, or on behalf of the families of those killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the second paragraph of your statement that reads: "Serbian volunteer, Sergeant Dragoljub Kuveljic, born 21 September 1090 (as written), in Bijelo Polje, Montenegro, a participant in the war of liberation and defence from 5 July 1992 to 9 October 1995, when he was wounded during the liberation of Kljuc in the Republika Srpska as a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guards." Apart from the error in the person's year of birth, is this statement accurate?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the information I was provided by Dragoljub Kuveljic, because the military records office of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska sought this data.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge, based on your own experiences, of Mr. Kuveljic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He was a guardsman and stayed on much longer after I had to stop fighting because I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you discuss his wounding. Is it correct that Mr. Kuveljic was wounded on the 9th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes. He wrote that to me and showed me a certificate issued by the hospital which had taken him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you personally know that based on your role in the Guard in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His heroic act was much talked about in the Guard. He was wounded as he was trying to save his wounded fellow fighter. I think that he was even decorated for that, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Djoko Djekic died during the same attack on 9 October 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a volunteer from Republika Srpska. And I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this statement, you also refer to an individual named Rade. Could you please provide us with this individual's full name and nickname?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I know that that was the person that Kuveljic had tried to rescue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have the second page of this exhibit in both B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is this the handwritten statement that was provided to you by Mr. Kuveljic, which was attached to your letter?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the first paragraph on this page, is it correct that Aleksandar Drazovic died on the 4th of October, 1995, as indicated in this statement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I can see it under the photograph of the late Aleksandar, aka Hans, framed with other photographs hanging on the wall in my house, and you cannot expect me to know each and every name of all the 51 combatants of the Guard that were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 2D904 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Objection on the grounds of relevance. And secondly, that my learned friend needs to explain why this -- well, let me stick with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Relevance, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's relevant to establish who the Serbian Volunteer Guard members are who participated in combat operations in September and October 1995. It's centrally relevant to what's alleged in the indictment. These identities are important. That's why we asked about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say you would link those identities to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- other evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To other evidence. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would still submit that the witness's answers can then stand as the evidence. This is fresh evidence, and my learned friend -- if this issue was important to the Prosecution, they've had many years to investigate it. They've asked the witness questions. His evidence is there. There's no need for this fresh evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document we got last week from the Defence. It's never been available to us before, and the Simatovic Defence just handed it to us last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But it's the witness's evidence which is important. That's what my learned friend has suggested. This is a statement with lots of new evidence in it. If this statement is entered into evidence, we, the Defence, now have to seek to investigate its contents. Why do the Prosecution need it, when they've got the witness here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How could -- Mr. Jordash, I'm just trying to consider both positions. How could the Prosecution be aware of the knowledge of this witness without this statement in relation to this specific element of who was at that point in time known to this witness as being a member of the SDG? Isn't it true that the case law on -- on fresh evidence has got something to do also with availability of that evidence at a certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, that's right. If it is truly the case that it's important to the Prosecution which members of Arkan's Tigers took part in Sanski Most and Banja Luka, then that was an issue which ought to have been investigated. First of all, that should have been noticed to the Defence. Who was it, they say, as individuals, the accused are responsible for? That should have been investigated a long time ago. If it is their case that the individual names are of critical importance, then we ought to have that indicated to us so that we, the Defence, can respond to that. If there are other facts within this statement which are important to the Prosecution, and that, in reality, must be the case, then we ought to have notice of what significance those facts play in their case. Rather than asking a witness a few questions on very narrow issues relating to identity, then putting a statement in without any explanation, not just to the Defence, but with the Court. What's the probative value of the remainder of this statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is -- Let me first ask Mr. Bakrac. Anything that you would like to add? Or do you agree with Mr. Jordash or do you disagree with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I appreciate Mr. Jordash's views, but this was anyway added to our 65 ter list once we received it from Mr. Pelevic. This is just a sample of a statement that Mr. Pelevic gave in Republika Srpska in order to prove his pensionable service, and we have no objection to its being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that is -- you say you appreciate Mr. Jordash's views, but you have no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If that's my learned friend for Mr. Simatovic's position, he's explained precisely what this document is supposed to prove and therefore I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's ready for being admitted. Now, of course, the Chamber would also carefully look when interpreting a document for the purposes of making determinations it has to make. We'll also always carefully look at the circumstances under which it was introduced. But this should not be understood as a commitment that in the totality of the evidence we would under all circumstances limit ourselves to the reasons given, different reasons given by the parties. That -- I hope that that's clear for both Defence and Prosecution. Then, Madam Registrar, what would be the number? I didn't hear a confirmation yet, but the body language was such that I considered that the parties did agree. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D904 will receive number P3069, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 2D518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for that, could I ask you,

utterances.speaker: MR. PELEVIC
utterances.text: The report we just saw on the screen, how Mr. Kuveljic got wounded, what happened exactly at the front line, you have no personal knowledge of that, do you? It's just what you -- what you received as information, you then put that on paper. And as you explained, it is partly what was given to you in writing and that it was, if I understand you well, it was notorious general knowledge at the time within the SDG.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. But I also saw the document produced by the hospital in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which, of course, I was mainly focussing on what happened at the front line rather than what people saw in hospital. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you, I believe, is another form that you produced to the Defence for Radnov Zarica; is that correct, that this is one of the forms that you produced?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, Mr. Prosecutor, this is Zarica as the last name, but the first name should be Radovan. Actually, Zarica is his first name and Radnov is his last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I wanted to clarify that with you. Is this one of the documents you produced to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any other documents related to this individual?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. Only I have a photo of him at my home, with all his personal details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Whose handwriting appears in the upper-right corner of the document? If you need the original, I do have the original here with me in court, if you'd like to view it.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that. How do you expect me to know who wrote this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did this individual -- was he killed on the 7th of October, 1995, in Kljuc? Do you have personal knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our units, together with the special brigade of the MUP of Republika Srpska, besieged Kljuc at the time, and that's for sure. That is when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And you know that Mr. Radnov died during that operation, personally?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, as I said, but I don't know what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear of his death?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D518 will receive number P3070.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. P3070 is admitted into evidence. Could the Chamber have a look at the original, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if at this time I could also provide a copy of the next document I'm going to show to the witness. I have the original on that, but I'll provide that to the Court Usher to also deliver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. We have to take a break at 3.30, as I said before, for reasons unrelated to the situation of Mr. Stanisic. But before you go to the next document, I would have one question for you. Mr. Pelevic, why is it that you have the originals in your possession, and how many of those do you have? Only of the deceased? Or of other members as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I have the photographs of all our killed men in my house, and in an envelope as well, because we used to publish obituaries in the papers on the day of their death. Apart from that, I have nothing else. Whatever I had I gave to the Defence and to the Serbian War Crimes Prosecutor's Office, Chief Prosecutor Vukcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So may I then take it that these documents of those members who had died were taken out of the normal administration and would then be with you; whereas for members who are still alive, that they were kept with the SDG administration? Or ... Where are similar copies of those who had not died?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I already said that after Arkan's death, in his office I found in his desk a number of such documents and I took them to my home for safekeeping, because after his death this office was no longer his. I have no other documents relating to those still living, but the list of those who died and -- or were wounded and the families of those who had died I handed over to Mr. Vukcevic at the Serbia's War Prosecution Office. He has everything in his possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break, and will be a break a little bit longer than usual; it will be 40 minutes. So we'll resume at ten minutes past 4.00. And I return the original to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, before the break you did not have a full session of 75 minutes. Could you -- so, therefore, you get a little bit more time, but could you try to proceed as efficiently as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, earlier today we discussed codes used by the Serbian Volunteer Guard. You mentioned that yours was the number 22 and Arkan's was 99. Do you know what Legija's code was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His code was "Tiger 01."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 2D521. And at this time, Your Honour, I'd ask the Court Officer to please provide the witness with the original copy of this document that we have in court. I do not know if Your Honours would like to view the document first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if it's a similar one as the previous one, then there is no need. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, is it correct that before you is another form that you produced to the Simatovic Defence, this one related to Aleksandar Manojlovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any additional documentation for this individual?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I do want to note for the record that I have absolutely no idea the relevance of this individual or who he is said to be commanded by or in which locations or which crimes he's supposed to have committed -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask questions. I ask that Mr. Jordash at least wait until I tender the document if he's going to enter these objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's unclear to Mr. Jordash at this moment, so, therefore, it should be -- you should attempt to make that clear as possible. Because if it's unclear to Mr. Jordash, it might be unclear to the Chamber as well at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from that, I've got one -- you referred to Legija. Now I am - it will not surprise you - familiar with Milorad Ulemek, Legija. But today a Legija was linked to another name, and I wanted to avoid whatever confusion that might arise. And I have to find it - one second - today's transcript -- I think it was today, but ... although the first name was Milorad as well, it was a different family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it may be that it's "Lukovic," which is, as I understand, another name of the same Legija. But it was not then -- it was -- he was referred to only as "Lukovic" and not as "Ulemek." But we're talking about the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Legija changed his last name twice. His real last name was "Ulemek," but when he got married he took his wife's last name "Lukovic." And then after the divorce, he reverted to his original name of "Ulemek."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, that may have -- I'm so familiar with "Ulemek" that I missed that, although that's -- other members of the Bench are better in this respect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, is the document in your hands a photocopy with a picture attached, and then does have it some handwriting on it in the upper-right corner and at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know whose handwriting appears on that page?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. It's not mine, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the upper-right corner, is it correct that the date of death on this document has been changed with the number 2 crossed out and written over in blue ink with the number 1? And then also the location of death, has that been changed, crossing out the word "Sanski Most," which I believe is much more visible in the original before you, and writing the word "Mrkonjic Grad" next to it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that these corrections were made, both with regard to the date and the place of where he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know whose phone numbers are at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see here that his residential address is Stara Pazova. I think that 022 is a code number for Stara Pazova, because the capital of Vojvodina, Novi Sad, has the area code number 021, and I suppose that this telephone number belongs to his parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the section that reads "date of arrival in the Guards," it states "20 June 1995." Do you know whether Mr. Manojlovic participated in the Trnovo operations in July 1995, after he arrived?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't be able to know that. He was accepted on the 20th of June, 1995. I didn't know him personally, and I don't know whether it was possible for him to be sent to Trnovo, because it took place at that time approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can you confirm, based on your own knowledge of what you heard or the records that you have kept, whether or not this individual died as a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard at the beginning of October 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any specific knowledge, but I can give you an answer only after I have checked this framed set of photographs of members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, whether he was among them or not. I cannot give you all the names of those people, particularly those who joined the Guard after me. And, as you can see, this was in mid-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe that this document is inaccurate and that this individual did not die as a member of the Guard in October 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that I wasn't there, I cannot confirm that. But I could -- would kindly ask you to accept a proposal that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Before --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A resolution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, perhaps you first answer the question. The question was not whether he died, but whether you have any reason to believe that what is in this document, that it's inaccurate. So that you say, Well, that sounds illogical, or that's ... I mean, is there any reason why you would believe that this document would not be accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have no reason. And it doesn't make sense, as you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution tenders 2D521 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we deal with that, the witness was about to make a proposal, and I think we should give him an opportunity to make that proposal. Whether or not we'll accept it is a different matter, Mr. Pelevic. But tell us what your proposal -- what proposal you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that your investigators working in Belgrade go to my home and verify there whether he was within this frame of all the combatants who were killed and which contains all their personal data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have a counter-proposal. If you do not find him at home in the frame, it might be wise to inform Mr. Bakrac about that. Would that be a proposal which the party could support and accept? Because usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we do not give witnesses tasks for after they have concluded their testimony, but ... Mr. Jordash, the proposal is that the witness, if he doesn't find this person in his frame at home, that he informs Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, my -- my problem with all of this is, as I've indicated, is that the Prosecution have not indicated the significance and the relevance and the probative value of this evidence. My learned friend is silent and will persist on being silent on this issue because either he's investigating for a different case or he wants to keep his case as private as possible so he can ambush the Defence. I mean, Mr. Weber should indicate what this person is alleged to have done and their connection to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the -- I would say that's the same objection you expressed for the last one. Could we make the proposal conditional on admission into evidence of these two documents? I mean, it doesn't make much sense to send the witness with a -- that's one. Second is, Mr. Bakrac, would you object the counter-proposal -- or would you object to the proposal?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I am prepared to hear from Mr. Pelevic once he goes back home whether he managed to find this photo or not, and then I will convey this information to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not necessarily to the Chamber, but at least that it's -- that the parties have this information available. We'll consider whether we accept your proposal or whether we'll suggest to you or invite you to do what the counter-proposal would require. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- tender the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibit gets a number and will then be -- the last one, let me just check, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is -- the Prosecution is tendering 2D521.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would receive number ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on admission ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I just -- for the record, I object to the tendering of it. It doesn't comport with Your Honours' guidance delivered on the 26th of August, 2011. And absent any indication what the Prosecution's -- significance of this individual to the Prosecution case, not only -- well, we cannot investigate. I don't know what to do with this. And I doubt very much, respectfully, that anyone else in this room does either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please assign a number. The document will be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D521 will receive number P3071, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 2D526. If I could also ask the Court Officer to retrieve the original of the last document from the witness. For the record, at the end of today's hearing the Prosecution will return the originals of these documents to the Simatovic Defence, unless the Chamber would like them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not in need of receiving the -- keeping the originals. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- before -- I mean, I know I'm likely to lose the argument, but nonetheless for the record I do want to note that we have moved from a circumstance where once upon a time when the Prosecution wanted to use a document they had to lay a foundation, and they had to lay a foundation which was consistent with Your Honour's guidance which I've referred to, and actually lay a foundation as to why they wanted to use a new document. We've now moved to a situation where the Prosecution simply pull out a document from wherever and use it without any explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just mention one thing for the record. I believe that the context that have allowed the discussions and objections that are happening right now is in the issue of fresh evidence. And it is my recollection of the law on this that fresh evidence constitutes something that is not on an exhibit list of a party. The documents I am using do come from an exhibit list, that being the Simatovic Defence exhibit list. If I'm wrong with that, then I might -- I might be, but I'm simply -- these documents were not documents that were available to the Prosecution as part of its own case; they were available to an individual Defence witness, produced to a Defence team, and included on a Defence exhibit list. This individual is now testifying, and the Prosecution should be entitled to use documents that are from the Defence exhibit list to put to the witness about his own personal knowledge of records that are in his own collection relating to activities that surround an alleged incident in the indictment. And we have alleged crimes that were committed in the fall of 1995 in the vicinity of Sanski Most. So I believe that we're having a lot of discussions here over something that the Prosecution submits does not have much merit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, at this moment, we have marked the last document for identification. The previous document was admitted into evidence after we had heard the parties. And -- but the Chamber will further consider, and perhaps at the end of today's session we might find some additional time to deal with it, but the Chamber will consider -- of course, when considering to admit this document into evidence, and if the outcome would be negative, it might lead -- it might trigger the Chamber to reconsider its previous decision as well. So we have to look at it in more detail, whether -- there are quite a few elements which are different from previous situations. I mention only one document on the exhibit list, of course, where I think in the guidance was a reference to documents that had been on the exhibit list for a while, and not since yesterday. There are a few matters which we would like to further consider, and we might seek the guidance of the parties in that respect as well. At this moment, the document, the second of the personal cards, is now marked for identification, and we may want to reconsider our decision on P3070 as well. Let's proceed for the time being. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the record, before the witness is 65 ter 2D526.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, is this another document you've produced to the Defence of Mr. Simatovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I have the originals here that were provided to me by the Simatovic Defence of the documents that you provided. Would you like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do the parties agree on that this document was provided to the Simatovic Defence by the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we agree. This is what we had in the form of a note as having come from Mr. Pelevic and received by Mr. Jovanovic. So that was part of the file we had, it was in a plastic sleeve, and we handed it all to Mr. Weber as we had it, and it has been on our 65 ter list since June 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jordash, any dispute about whether this was received from this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we proceed, where the parties have no dispute about the source of this document. It is received from the witness, as I understand, most likely by the late Mr. Jovanovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this document is a certificate on the circumstances surrounding the wounding of a Dejan Velickovic. From your own knowledge, are you able to say whether or not this individual was wounded as a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it states here that he joined the Guard in the month of August 1995 and that he was from Republika Srpska. I wasn't able to know all the guardsmen, and I don't know this individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any reason to believe that this individual was not a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard between 11 August 1995 and when he was wounded on 21 October 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Does the B/C/S version before you indicate that this document was sent to the "arhivi" and not sent to files?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. The only thing it says here is internal number. It doesn't say either the archives or the records. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the text on the bottom on the lower left, does that text indicate this certificate was sent to archives?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It says "archives." I didn't see it before. Believe me, it's in a very small print.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. We've already discussed what you know about the archives of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. Do you know if this certificate would have gone to any other archives besides those of the SDG?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, let me just check now what caused the -- You are more or less contesting the translation implicitly. So before we start a whole line of questioning on the difference between archives and files, I'd first like to clarify whether -- whether there is any inconsistency between the two. Is the word "arhivi," is it possible to translate it as "files" as well? Or does it exclusively mean "archives"? Then the next question would be: What's the difference between files and archives? So that's all implicit here. And I would like to -- to avoid any confusion in this respect. Because if you say, "Isn't it true it's archives, not files?" then, of course, you are more or less burdening the witness with something that should be dealt with elsewhere. That is, with CLSS. Therefore, I -- it confuses me, and I'd like you to avoid that I get confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, are -- in the Serbian language, are the words "archives" and "files" two different words?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, documentation is something that is used at -- currently, so something that is part of your current affairs, that you're working on; whereas, something that you would file in an archive is something that you've dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Can the word "arhivi" be interpreted or translated as the word "files" in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, of course, how could we -- then we depend, for the answer to this question, we depend how the interpreters have translated that word, and that's exactly the issue at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, it is not a real -- it's -- it doesn't clarify matters. There is a fundamental other question. Apparently, Mr. Weber, you consider it as a possibility that something, already at the moment when it is produced, would immediately sent to archives, which would mean that it does not assist them of current storing of documentation but that it would be sent to a -- the type of storage which we usually refer to as archiving. Now, that is, at least for me, a novelty, because usually documents are first stored in -- whether you call it files or documentation, et cetera, and then after a certain period of time when you think you don't need them on an occurring basis anymore you send them to the archives. That's at least my understanding of these words. Now, if my understanding is correct, then apart from the linguistic matter which could be raised here, there's also a systematic question that you could raise. Having no administrative files and send matters immediately to the archive is, of course, something -- well, I would love to hear experience of other professionals on how that works so that I better understand what it means that you send a document immediately to the archives. It -- I just share with you some of my problems in understanding your questions, possible answers, and the document itself. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll address the matter with CLSS.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, sir, my question to you is: Do you know if this would have been -- this document would have been kept by anyone besides the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no reason for me to believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution at this time tenders the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just repeat my objection. I have absolutely no idea what happened just then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification as well. We'll consider it in the context of the other documents. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D526 will receive number P3072, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, in the documents that we just looked at, the names "Dragoljub Kuveljic," "Djoko Djekic," "Zarica, Radnov," "Aleksandar Manojlovic," and "Dejan Velickovic" were mentioned. Is it your evidence that these individuals were members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am absolutely certain when it comes to Kuveljic. And I would have to check for the other two. I can't state that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I just mentioned five names. How about Djoko Djekic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Zarica Radnov?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw his file, and he was definitely in the Guard. I don't know for how long, though, because people came and went.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Aleksandar Manojlovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see that he was in the Guard, but I don't know for how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dejan Velickovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't seen his file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Why would you have these files in your possession if they were not members of the SDG?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I've already said that everything I found in the drawer of the desk of late Arkan I took home with me for safekeeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did these individuals work for any other organisation besides the Serbian Volunteer Guard?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which type of organisation you have in mind. Military? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I mean any other organisation aside from the Serbian Volunteer Guard.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have knowledge to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you saying that because you are -- because you definitively know they were not a part of any other organisation besides the Serbian Volunteer Guard; or are you simply saying you don't know, and they may have been?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Mr. Jordash, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please, if I may. There's one subject which I'd like to raise, if I may. It's not strictly arising from Mr. Weber's cross-examination, but it's something that I wanted to ask the witness about in relation to Banja Luka, with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the five extra minutes you're ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You can start your questions. And then if at a certain moment we would -- then knowing what it is about, because Banja Luka is just a geographical indication, then we could - the emphasis is on "could" - reconsider. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just a few questions, if I can, Mr. Pelevic. You testified on the 25th of January to the sending of SDG forces to the Banja Luka region in September and October of 1995. You recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you testified that there were 200 volunteers who were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that was, Your Honours, page 16433.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall properly, I said around 200. I don't know the exact number. You know that there were more or less 200 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, that's what I want to ask you about. Because a witness in this court first claimed that 100 men had been sent to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's at, Your Honours, P1615.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then when the witness gave evidence a bit later on, the witness claimed that 3- to 4 00 of Arkan's men had been sent to Banja Luka. And I want to try to understand how much -- how certain you are that only around 200 were sent. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Defence Counsel, as we were able to see in the video footage of the 10th of October, 1995, when the celebration was going on of the Guard, there were around 200 men present there. We could not have sent either 300 or 400 men because that was far more than we had at our disposal. And we had around 200. Something that Arkan spoke about as well. Was it more, was it less? I don't know. What I definitely know is that there weren't 100, but there weren't 300. And even less were there 400 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, you know that, then, because Arkan himself said - is this right? - that there were around 200 Tigers at that point in time; is that right? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you understand me correctly. But don't forget that I also said that I was visiting the Guard and Commander Arkan for some three or four days and that during my visit to the guardsmen I was able to see for myself that there weren't many more than 200 or fewer than 200 at the time. I know that because I spent time with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you visited them where precisely, and in what circumstances, which enabled you to say with such certainty that there was 200, around 200, or maybe even less?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our Guard had the front end of the positions on the hill called Cadjevica, facing the Muslim forces. That's where they were stationed and where they were dug in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Take us there. You went there. How did you know, how were you able to say -- I'm not disagreeing with you. I just want to understand precisely how you are so sure that there was around 200. What did you see to indicate that to you or what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I spent some five or six days there. I can't be sure. It was shortly after the celebration event where I spoke, in addition to Commander Arkan. I went to visit our positions there, and one day something happened that nobody had expected. The Serb forces started withdrawing. Even our forces holding the positions at Cadjevica began retreating. Both the commander and I were attending a meeting in Banja Luka at the time. We left right away for that position, where we found General Momir Talic. The two of them agreed that they would proceed to Manjaca right away to prevent the Serbian forces from retreating, because should a single Serb soldier have entered Banja Luka, the same scenario would have happened as had happened in Knin. All the Serbs from the Banja Luka Krajina would have attempted to flee across the Drina as did the Krajina Serbs in 1995. We were successful. I was next to Commander Arkan who was driving in the jeep. There was General Momir Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, and I was there with them in the jeep, on our way there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe I've missed it, but why then -- how did this enable you to see with such certainty that there was only 200? And slow down a little bit, too. The translator is chasing you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Counsel, I told you that I toured our guards on the positions on some five or six occasions, and it wasn't difficult for me as an experienced soldier to gauge how many of our volunteers were there. We also spoke about it in Banja Luka with the commander. So I don't see how I would have made such a big mistake. I could not have been mistaken by more than ten men, take it or leave it. But that was my estimate of around 200 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. I'll take it, if you don't mind, and I'll move on. The next subject I want to -- and the only subject I want to ask you about now is the training and the numbers of men who were trained. Earlier today you said that you "can't claim that there were 10.000 people exactly, but there was several thousand men who went through the Guards ... were trained. They first had a one-month period there, and then a three-months' period."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then later you said -- or a couple of lines later, you said, when asked -- sorry, you said this: "But throughout the period of my time, my assessment would be that there were about 10.000 of them." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I recall what exactly? My answer or how many men there had been?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, let's just assume you do recall your evidence today about training. Where were, in general, these men trained? We know that there's a training camp, according to you, at Erdut. Was there any other training camps, or was Erdut the principal training camp for the Guards?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me to say this, I did not keep precise records of the men who went through training. I had other duties to attend. As for the location of the training courses: Physical fitness training was conducted, in part, in Erdut along the stretch all the way to Dalj, some 20 kilometres, because it involved running. Now, the part of the training which had to do with the fitness and martial arts took place on the training grounds within our centre. This was a large lawn with hurdles that any elite unit in the world has to go through. As for marksmanship, this was taking place not far from the centre, and there was full cover all around in the form of various buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, obviously if -- sorry, let me go back. You -- you -- you suggest that about 10.000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could we first get a better answer to your last question. Erdut was the centre. Training took place in that centre and just around that centre. You -- okay. Was there any other such centre where similar training was given? At a distant location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're thinking that it was in the territory of some other municipality, then the answer is no. Our centre was in the municipality of Erdut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was the only centre which provided for such training, where people were accommodated in the centre, although part of the training took place outside the limits of the premises of the centre itself. That's, Mr. Jordash, I think you were interested to know, not whether the running was five miles out of the centre. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we have an answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And are you able to -- I know this may be asking a bit much, but 10.000 people over a five-year period, from 1991 to 1995, are you able to divide that up into years, how many men were being trained per year during that five-year period, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the witness invited to divide a thousand -- 10.000 by 5?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we could give the answer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, no, sorry. It's my lack of clarity on -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what your question is about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it's more whether perhaps there was 9.000 in 1991. But I'm just trying to work out the -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If that's what you -- so you would say, "Was there an equal division of those trained over the years?" That's then your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if not, then how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- how many per year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then that's a clear question now. Could you answer the question, witness, whether there were more busy times and less busy times over those years in training, or whether it was on average more or less the same over the years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since after I had been wounded in early February 1993, I wasn't able to conduct any further training. I cannot give you an exact answer. I can tell you how it was during the period starting from when I came, that is, the whole of 1992, because already in January we left for the Benkovac front. But I have to say that I wasn't much bothered with counting people or keeping records. All I can say is that approximately -- well, the question you're asking me is very difficult. But let's say that my rough estimate would be 1.000 men or 1200 men. But I honestly can't give you an accurate answer because I was not involved in these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So I understand that correctly, or so the Court understands that correctly: 1.000 or 1.2 00 men in 1992; is that what you're suggesting? Or have I misunderstood that? I'm not pushing you for precise, just to clarify what approximate figure you've just given, and for which year.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made an oath to this Court to speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. However, you are putting me into a situation that I might inadvertently tell an untruth. This is my rough estimate. I can't give you an exact number. And my estimates might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: For nineteen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The issue is, What is the estimate about? The 1.000 or 1200 men you mentioned, accepting that it's a rough estimate, was that the number of men as trained in 1992 in the centre according to your rough estimate? Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what happened to all these men? They didn't all join the Tigers. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are. Some were unable to pass the training and were sent home. A number of the recruits who arrived changed their mind after undergoing these difficult training and left on their -- of their own accord. Please realize that the first contracts were signed for a month and after that we proceeded with three-month contracts, which means that people would come, stay there for three months, and then leave, because they would realize that, having undergone such a difficult training, they were not fit for the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And presumably some went and joined other units, military units, or TO units or paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases of that nature. Not many of them, but there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you gave evidence, I think two days ago, that this training had nothing to do with the Serbian DB. Did this training -- so I won't revisit that, but did this training camp have anything to do with any other training camp? Were you ever asked, for example, by anybody to link this training camp to another training camp in the Eastern Slavonia or in the Knin region, or was it completely autonomous?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre was completely autonomous. We didn't want anyone to be linked with us, because we had a remarkably well-developed system of training, both physical and mental.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that my estimate that I had given you before the break still stays.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Pelevic. It's evening already. I'll try to take no more than ten or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Weber asked you about the checks that were made when you applied to join the Serbian Volunteer Guard, and you answered that you said that you know that somebody went to your work organisation to make inquiries about you and also at the kick-box association of Yugoslavia. You also said that you don't know whether anyone went to make these checks with the MUP. When you were being promoted within the party and the Serbian Volunteer Guard, do you know that when you accepted candidates whether any vetting procedures were carried out within the MUP regarding these candidates?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was absolutely no vetting procedure conducted with the MUP. We only wanted each and every member of the Guard to provide a certificate that he doesn't have any prior criminal convictions, and that could easily have been obtained. I know that because --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last portion of his answer and slow down, if possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last portion of your answer starting with: "I know that because ..." And then say what you said a second ago. And could you slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that because I closely co-operated with the head of the office in Belgrade, Mr. Jovan Dimitrijevic, and I would surely know about that, because he was the one who admitted the recruits.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we have to go back because it was not properly record in the transcript, and I'm going to repeat my question. You said that you know that in certain instances some individuals were required to provide certificates that they had no prior convictions, and you said that these certificates could be obtained from where?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each citizen of Serbia can have this certificate issued by the local court in Serbia, in the places where they live.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic. Mr. Weber showed you Exhibit P2616 - we don't need to have it back on the screen, and I think that all the parties will agree that I can summarize it - to the effect that this was produced by the administration -- security administration of the Yugoslav army. And it was sent to the RSK, that Arkan's Tigers were going -- and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat and slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you are invited by the interpreters to repeat the remainder of your question and to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will. Thank you. I apologise to the interpreters' booths.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I paraphrased and it was not recorded that the security administration of the Yugoslav army based in Belgrade sent to the Army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina a report that Arkan's Tigers were going to Zadar in order to plunder the place and that each one of them was receiving a monthly payment of 5.000 German marks. In this same document it is also said that this report should be checked. So this was what you could have seen from document P2616 shown by Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have document D69, and can we zoom in on the letterhead for starters. While we are waiting, I'm going try to read it. It says: "Republic of Serbian Krajina, Main Staff of the Serbian army. Information about the situation on the North Dalmatian front in the Republic of Serbian Krajina." So we have before us a document which was produced by the staff of the Army of the Serbian Krajina. Can we go to the last paragraph in B/C/S. And, Your Honours, in English, it's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I am going to read it out to and I will ask you to confirm, given that you were on this front, whether this information provided by the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2 in English, please, the top of the page, for the benefit of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is 28th January 1993. It reads -- now we have the English version as well. "In the opinion of soldiers and people of Obrovac, the arrival of Arkan and his volunteers was welcomed with enthusiasm. This was the chief reason why many people started returning to their homes, while in combat terms, with skillful tactical moves, he made combat operations useful, and the situation in Obrovac has been fully consolidated." This is a document authored by Assistant Commander Colonel Kosta Novakovic. Mr. Pelevic, does this document, this report relating to the engagement of the Serbian Volunteer Guard on the Benkovac front, reflect your personal experience?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this is a report from the Main Staff of the Serbian army sent to all the corps of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina and all the press centres in Knin, Topusko, and Vukovar, this is an accurate description of the situation. In other words, this completely refutes the reports of the so-called intelligence service of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina, because this information in this report was provided by the Main Staff, which testifies that the soldiers and the population of Obrovac welcomed enthusiastically the arrival of Arkan and his volunteers, and it also contributed to the incentive given to people to return home, and I personally was a witness to all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, my learned friend, Mr. Weber, asked you about the bringing in of deserters in the area of Banja Luka Krajina. If I remember correctly, you said that that was done pursuant to an order of Mr. Kovac and that it lasted for a short period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now have Exhibit D28.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, I will tell you that this is a -- an order sent by dispatch on the 11th of October, 1995.
