It was sent from the office of the minister of the MUP of Republika Srpska, and it says: [As read] "Pursuant to the agreement between the MUP minister and the chief of the Serbian Army of Republika Srpska, Manojlo Milovanovic, I hereby order that the chief of the Prijedor CJB, commander of the Tigers, Zeljko Raznjatovic, and the commander of the Janja detachment shall immediately start arresting deserters from the front in the territory of the Prijedor CJB, organise them in military ranks, and return them to their original brigade. This task should be carried out together with unit commands. If they are in the area and if they are not, further command should be agreed with the Main Staff." Is this the order issued by Tomo Kovac that you mentioned and which relates to the sending back of deserters?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that this order was issued based on an agreement between the MUP minister, Mr. Kovac, and the Chief of the Main Staff, Manojlo Milovanovic, but all the better. And, of course, we had to obey this order. It was not our will. We didn't go there to arrest anyone, but, rather, to fight side by side with them in order to liberate the Banja Luka Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... could I first seek -- I'm trying to fully understand the evidence given by the witness. Mr. Bakrac, you took us back to the evidence about the allegations that Arkan's units would be not interested in defending the territory, but in taking control of Zadar in order to loot the local banks, et cetera, and that was the bad reception of what people would think Arkan would do. And then you then took us to the other document, if I understood you well, to demonstrate how welcome Arkan's troops were. Is that correct? Now, the first one was about what Arkan was expected to do in Zadar. And the other document was about how people welcomed Arkan in Benkovac, if I'm ... is that correct? Could we then try to get a clear picture of the situation. Witness, could you tell me: When Arkan arrived in Benkovac, where everyone -- where he even enabled people to return to their homes, who would return to their homes? I mean, who had apparently left the area before, who would now return to their homes? Were those Croats? Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the attack on Maslenica, there were quite a few refugees, almost the entire population of Obrovac, a location close to Knin, fled, and they were the Serbian population. On our arrival in Obrovac and Benkovac, a great many of them returned. As the document states, this boosted the morale of the Army of of -- the Army of Republika Srpska in this western area of the Krajina. That's to say, in the Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it has to do with the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, upon arrival of Arkan, Serbs could return and were quite happy that they could return because the area was brought under Serb control again. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the other document dealt with what people feared Arkan's people would do in Zadar. What was the majority of the population in Zadar? Was it Serb? - at that point in time - was it Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the history, Zadar had always had more Croats than Serbs. So it was the majority Croat population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not talking about history. I'm talking about that point in time which was -- where, I think, major portions - but please correct me when my understanding is wrong - when major portions of the Krajina had become under Serb control; whereas other parts of the costal area were still under Croat control. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did many Serbs remain in Zadar at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of the Serbs in Zadar had fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, my question to you is the following: Comparing how welcome Arkan was after Serbs had taken control again of that area, to compare that with the fears of the population in Zadar, which was mainly Croat, would the one be -- would the one way of receiving Arkan and his troops being very welcome, would that demonstrate that in Croat areas he would be similarly welcome?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, our forces would never have been welcome in the Croatian areas, but there was no interest on -- on the part of any Serb authority to occupy Zadar. It was a Croatian town.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not saying any of -- I'm not saying that -- I'm not commenting on whether he intended, yes or no. The only thing I want to draw your attention to, Mr. Bakrac, is that how welcome Arkan may have been in Obrovac and Benkovac, that the situation there, as the witness explained to us now, was quite different from where, apparently, people were in fear of Arkan. So to that extent it -- at least it's my understanding - but please elicit further evidence with the witness if my understanding is wrong, and it's provisional understanding, of course - that the one situation is difficult to compare with the other situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may have made a mistake, because I didn't show the relevant document to save time. The document that my learned friend Mr. Weber referred to was P2616. Let's have a look at it. And while we're waiting, it's the security organ of the SFRY of the JNA sent, an unverified piece of information to the Army of the RSK, wherein it is stated that Arkan went to the Knin front line with the intention of occupying Zadar and looting the local shops. Now, we have a document which proves quite the opposite, and that was the point I was trying to make. It reads here that the information is being forwarded in order to be checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that. Whether the one proves the other to be wrong is further to be considered, of course, in looking at the evidence in its entirety. By the way, when you quoted from that, the 5.000 German marks, you said per month, and that was done before today. It's now the second time, but that's, of course, not what the document says. The document says 5.000 Deutschemarks. That's all. Not any time-frame. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My intention was to show that the staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina had its own views, with regard to Arkan's forces, quite apart from what may have arrived from Belgrade to be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the topic that we were dealing with before these discussions. Let's have a look at 1D1607. Let me remind you that D28 of the 11th of October, 1995 -- or, rather, that's the date --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1607 is Exhibit D525, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I neglected to make that note. My apologies to Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The date is the 12th of October, 1995, in this document. Again, we have the MUP of Republika Srpska, minister's office, order, which reads: "The Tigers unit should discontinue taking in deserters. It should, rather, withdraw and prepare for combat. "These policing duties as well as others will be taken from -- will be taken on by members of the public security Prijedor together with the MUP units of Serbia." Mr. Pelevic, when you said that at one point your unit was no longer charged with bringing in deserters, did you have in mind this order by Kovac?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. When I arrived in Banja Luka, the commander told me that they couldn't wait to receive that sort of order sooner because they didn't want to have to deal with deserter but, rather, to engage in combat in order to defend the Banja Luka Krajina. In other words, this order was received with delight.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for the time you've given me. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to one hour and a half. We have to deal with a few matters on admission into evidence. I have a few questions for the witness. You have more questions for the witness as well, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- Your Honour, actually, the Prosecution just wanted to address one matter with respect to the proposal of checking the photograph in Mr. Pelevic's house, and we just wanted to tender exhibits that had been not provided to the Registry earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which gives an opportunity to the Chamber also perhaps to briefly think about a few matters which arose in court. And I also have to read a statement. So we will not finish in the next four minutes. There's no way of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. And could I -- I hesitate because I don't want to detain the Court, it's been a long day, but I do -- I would like to make very brief submissions about Rule 90(H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rule 90(H). Then I suggest that we take the break now. That, after the break, that I'll start with some questions that -- if my colleagues have any questions, that -- any further questions triggered by the questions by the Bench or questions Mr. Weber apparently has not at this very moment. And then we'll deal with the technicalities, admission into evidence, of some 90(H), and then at the very I'll read the statement. That's our programme for after the break. We -- I think we can have a bit of a shorter break as usual and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first is about the video that was shown to you, and I think it was the anniversary of the SDG, where you described what you saw at 16 minutes and 20 seconds. And I read your answer: "To the left you can see General Marko Pejic, Peja, from the SDG, wearing a red beret; and to the right, with a blue beret, you can see General Obrad Stevanovic, the commander of the PJP." Do you remember that image, where you commented on it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the next question was asked: "When you say the PJP unit, which one?" And then you explained: "It's a unit from the Serbia MUP. The MUP in Serbia ..." And then you gave some further explanation. Why was General Obrad Stevanovic present during the celebration of the anniversary of the -- of the SDG? Why was he there? What was his role, what was his link to the SDG?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The special unit of the MUP of Serbia was deployed along the borders of Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem, on the one hand, and Serbia. The authorities in Serbia were perhaps afraid that the Croatian forces would attack the eastern part of the Krajina, just as they had done on the western part on the 5th of August. And they were part of the 11th Corps of the VRS, and this was one of the units. And since he was one of the units of the 11th Corps, as had been the SDG, he felt that he should be there as a guest. I didn't like seeing him there, but, of course, you can't ever chase away guests at a party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at a party it's usually the host who invites the guest, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody invited him, you see. I sent the invitations out. It was the command of the 11th Corps that was invited, and they may have forwarded the invitation to him, but he was not invited personally. And I am sure about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then another question. You -- let me find it. You told us that you were unaware when you came as a soldier to Erdut that Badza was appointed deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You also told us that he had visited Erdut several times. You saw him there several times.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the beginning of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When did you become aware that he was appointed deputy minister of the interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I learnt it on my return from the Krka monastery. Previously I had my military duties to perform, and we did not receive any newspapers in Erdut, so I wasn't kept very well informed. It must have been when I met him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you also testified that he came there exclusively in his capacity as TO chief in -- in SV -- the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. When he met with Arkan, you told us that you did not attend those meetings. Now, not attending the meetings and not being aware that he was appointed deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia, how could you know exactly in what capacity he came and what he discussed with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him wearing a uniform of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. He did not arrive in the police uniform of the MUP of Serbia. I don't know what they talked about because I was an ordinary soldier. Later on, Arkan told me that they had become the best of friends and that before my arrival there they were on good terms as fellow fighters, fellow soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I do understand that Arkan told you that. Then after a month would you then discuss in what capacity he had come and what the subjects of discussion had been? Then discuss with you, I mean.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This wasn't the subject of the discussion. It was only much later that Arkan and I became close. From what I know, he later on left the position of the commander of the Territorial Defence. He was replaced by someone called Trajkovic, I believe, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my question is: Was it then far later that -- or was it -- your answers, were they based on what you observed when Badza came and visited Erdut, primarily?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really don't know what they talked about. I do know that after his visits the army would psychologically be preparing for an imminent action, because he was the commander of the Territorial Defence force that we were a member of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you say even later on you would never -- became really acquainted with the subjects that were discussed between Arkan and Badza. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can only assume that it had to do with military issues, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. You told us in your testimony about punishment in Erdut and people who did not obey orders or people who drank too much alcohol. Now, I have one or two questions for you as far as misbehaviour of SDG members is concerned. Did you ever hear of any SDG member committing a murder?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you mean in combat or in civilian life?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's focus, first, on having committed a murder after he had joined the SDG and in the context of SDG activity.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, there were killings in combat. I didn't hear of any other murders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of persons being captured or at least detained and then murdered by Arkan and/or SDG members?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I never heard. But I did hear that there were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you never heard about any prisoner -- well, let's say not of Serb nationality, any prisoner being killed when in the custody of -- custody under the control of the SDG?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard that. We handed over the prisoners of war to the army, and they would in turn exchange them for the soldiers and officers captured by the Croatian army. We didn't have the facilities in Erdut where we would be holding soldiers. That's to say, prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any statements that no prisoners of war should be made? Meaning that if someone was in your custody, that you should not keep him in custody but that perhaps some other fate would be the fate of that person?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was one of the rules of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. That's to say, respect for prisoners and women, children, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Up till this moment, have you never heard about prisoners being killed where members of the SDG and/or Arkan were nearby and may have been involved in such killings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never witnessed anything of the sort, nor did I hear of anyone from the Serbian Volunteer Guard, and especially not Arkan, having been an eye-witness to something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was whether you ever, up till this moment, heard about such events. Not whether you heard it from SDG members or from Arkan, but in general.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such accounts published by the media in Serbia. And when I say "media," I mean media owned by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ever find it important for yourself to seek verification of those publications to form an opinion on what you apparently never heard from SDG members or from Arkan to try to find out whether there was any truth in such reports?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since newspapers carried stories containing accusations against Arkan, during the trial as well, whether they were true or not, and since there were such newspapers that were constantly opposed to us and to Arkan, I wanted to but had no other way of checking these accounts other than by talking to Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you asked Arkan specifically whether he had ever been involved in any event of killing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him about Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other events?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... more specifically, did you ever ask about events that may have happened in the -- in Slavonia, Baranja, or Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There could not have been war crimes committed there, because that was territory under our administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say your administration. What do you mean exactly by that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that it was under Serb authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Had it always been?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this Chamber heard evidence about Vukovar being taken. Are you familiar with the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was before my time in the Guard. But it was discussed a great deal within the Guard. The Guard never did go into Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But did Vukovar come under Serb control after it had been previously under Croat control?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But the Serbian Guard had never been deployed to Vukovar. After Luzac, we went to Erdut. That was at least what I was told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Erdut was -- was that -- had that always been under Serb control, or had it been under Croat control in earlier days?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was under Croatian control earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it was then taken by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the Serb population in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem was the majority population, and they would not, and did not, accept Croatian authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But when I said -- when I asked you in -- when you gave an answer, "I mean that it was under Serb authority," when I asked "Had it always been?" you said: "I believe so." But it was geographically part of the Republic of Croatia in earlier days, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. However, these were not borders. They were merely administrative boundaries between the different republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you also ask Arkan about a criminal record he may have had in other countries?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I heard a great deal about it and read a great deal, but I never asked him about it. I was absolutely not interested in that part of his life. I suppose that there is some truth in that. At one point he started talking about it, but I interrupted him. I absolutely didn't want to hear anything about it. I met him when I arrived in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mentioned him a hero, and you didn't want to know about perhaps other sides of the person?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I wasn't interested in that. Everyone is entitled to their own past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My last question is the following: All the press publications, you said, were politically motivated if they described crimes that would have been committed by SDG members. That's one. And, second, you said, well, war crimes could not have been committed in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem because it was under Serb control. Do I have to understand the last part of this answer that whether committed as war crimes or committed as crimes not directly related to war, in your view, but that the SDG, SDG members, including Arkan, were never involved in killings of people that were deprived of their liberty, that were in some kind of detention? And my question initially was whether you have -- had ever heard about such events: Detained people being killed in SBWS. Even if it was before you joined the SDG.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had not heard of any sort of war crimes in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. But I did hear of other forces committing war crimes in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "I had not heard of any sort of war crimes ..." My question, I make a clear distinction that I was not interested in whether you call them war crimes or whether you understood them to be war crimes. Had you ever heard of SDG members, including Arkan, being involved, even before you joined the SDG, being involved in the killing of persons detained in SBWS, irrespective of whether you considered that there was a war situation, but did you ever hear about such cases, such events?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what you describe is a serious war crime, but I had never heard of such an instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Whether I describe a war crime or whether I describe an ordinary crime, that is, murder, is -- we leave that apart from this moment. I describe a factual situation, and I ask you not to qualify what I describe, but I ask you whether you'd ever heard of a crime consisting of people being deprived of their liberty, so, therefore, in some kind of detention situation, being killed, where SDG members or Arkan was involved in such killings. And I'm focussing on SBWS even when it was before you joined the SDG. Did you ever hear about such a thing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I wasn't aware of that. I didn't hear about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Up till the day of today?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I heard of was that the Guard was accused of the events in Sanski Most and Zvornik, and I think that that's it. As for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, I never heard anything to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Up till the day of today.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you. Have the questions -- well, let me first ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Bench has no further questions for you. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's less that the questions have triggered further questions, but I've been informed by a B/C/S speaker in my team that there was an error or there may have been an error in the translation at page 128 of today's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 128. We'll check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it's the witness may have said something which may be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first find 128. I'm there. Could you point me to the line involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's somewhere between line 16 and 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the witness was talking about how he knew that there were only around 200 men in Banja Luka. And he may have said something which -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. What I'll do, I'll read his answer starting at line 16, or you do that, and then ask whether that reflects what he said, is -- whether anything is missing or whether anything is added which he didn't say, because that's then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your English is better, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, I just want to see if there's anything missing from the record we have of what you said earlier today when I was questioning you about the 200 men in Banja Luka. And the answer you gave was this, or one of the answers: "Mr. Counsel, I told you that I toured our guards on the positions on some five or six occasions, and it wasn't difficult for me to gauge how many of them were there. We also spoke about it in Banja Luka with the commander. So I don't see how I would have made such a large mistake. I could not have been mistaken by more than ten men, take it or leave it. But that was my estimate of around 200 men." Can you think carefully as to whether there was something else you said when expressing your position as to why you knew there was 200 men.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Esteemed Counsel, as far as I can see, the interpretation was bad probably due to the speed of my speech. I didn't say that our guards were on positions several times but that I visited them on the positions several times, which gave me an opportunity to learn their strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems not to be the problem because I, too, heard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did -- could I just ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's another possibility, Mr. Jordash. Of course, we always try to verify with the witness whether there are any mistakes. Of course, there is still the possibility that if really something is missing or ill-translated, then we can have that corrected by a request to CLSS. So if there's really an important matter which is misinterpreted, I'm always surprised that there's so little mistakes, but then you have other ways of verifying it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll deal with it that way. I think that's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes? Mr. Weber, usually we leave you as the last if it's a Defence witness. Anything you'd like to -- any question triggered by the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Not a question. But there was a discussion earlier about proposals, as to going -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first -- let's first clearly distinguish. This means that the testimony of this witness has been concluded hereby. And then we come to proposals, and we -- that is a matter which is, for me, a little bit distinct from -- from hearing evidence. And there are a few other matters as well, such as tendering and documents, and which some of them are now available. But for the proposal I think we still need the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, earlier today it was suggested a method as to how to have the witness check if certain individuals were on a board of photos in his house. The Prosecution actually, after further considering the discussion that happened earlier, it would be our preference to have an investigator from the Belgrade field office go and photograph whatever Mr. Pelevic would like us to look at in terms of this entire picture frame, and if that's okay with the witness, that would be our preferred -- our counter-proposal, I guess, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was his proposal: Send your investigators. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is linked to our submissions on 90(H).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say, We shouldn't have that evidence at all, so, well, why then send investigators and make photographs -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- of matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would put it slightly differently. That we -- the investigation would be legitimate if my learned friend had pursued his cross-examination in a different way, i.e., if he had complied with 90(H), and that's why I say that the two issues are linked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's clear. The Chamber will first hear submissions on, I would say, the legal issue involved. And there could be two legal issues involved. There's 90(H)(ii) and perhaps the fresh evidence issue there. It's a bit at the -- in the margin of these two issues. Let me just see. Do we need the witness for this? I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would prefer to have the submissions outside the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, witness, could I ask you to leave the courtroom for a second and wait outside. I promise that we'll not continue tomorrow, but at least the parties would like to bring a few matters to our attention. And it may have, I'm not saying it will have, but it may have an impact on proposal or counter-proposals. Could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The submission is that the Prosecution have violated Rule 90(H). The premise of the submission is based on four things that occurred during Mr. Weber's cross-examination. Number one, that he cross-examined on the subject matter of their case. Number two, the witness gave evidence which was contradictory to their case: and particularly today, at page 4, when the witness said that the relationship between Arkan's men and the DB wasn't a good one; at page 14 to 15, when he said that the DB was against the objectives of uniting the Serbian lands; and another example at page 54, that Arkan was against Ilija Kojic. Number three, that the Prosecution will later contest the case given by this witness by challenging his credibility or by adducing evidence to contradict it, and, in particular, but not limited to, the evidence, the fresh evidence, what we say is fresh evidence, related to the five men who the Prosecution will say were Arkan's men and were men who were under the control, in some way, of the DB. And, finally, fourth, that Mr. Weber at no time during his cross-examination, in general, or specifically, put the Prosecution's case concerning the DB's relationship with Arkan, let alone put their case in relation to Mr. Stanisic and Arkan and his men. Not a single word was said about Mr. Stanisic's relationship to Arkan, as alleged by the Prosecution. Not a single word was said about what must be a core part of their case, that the DB was in control of Arkan's men from 1991 throughout the indictment period. Those four facts are significant in light of Your Honours' guidance on Rule 90(H)(ii) and decision on Stanisic Defence submissions on Rule 90(H)(ii) dated 19th of October, 2011. I'm not going to detain the Court long, but to refer Your Honours to paragraphs 14 and 15 of that decision, and, in particular, paragraph 15, where Your Honours state: "The Chamber considers that Rule 90(H)(ii) is only applicable and then only in limited circumstances when a party cross-examines in category 3. Category 3 being contained in paragraph 14 as the subject matter of the cross-examining party's case if the witness is able to give relevant evidence." So 90(H)(ii) is applicable when the party cross-examines on that. In stating this, and I quote: "The Chamber stresses that the issue is not whether the evidence is contradictory to the cross-examining party's overall case, rather it is whether the witness's contradictory evidence given while being cross-examined in category 3 is later going to be contested by the cross-examining party introducing contradictory evidence or otherwise challenging the credibility of the witness's version of events." To summarize, what the Prosecution are seeking to do is to elicit certain evidence from this witness which is relevant to this case, and this fresh evidence is precisely on point, later seek to rely upon that evidence and say, Well, this witness, he would have known if these five men were Arkan's men. He, therefore, is support for our case that these men were Arkan's men, link that evidence up with other evidence to say, Arkan's men were controlled by the SDB. What they cannot do, in our submission, following Your Honour's guidance on Rule 90(H), 90(H)(ii), is take the good without complying with their obligations. And their obligations mean that once the witness has given evidence of that kind, which the Prosecution will later rely upon, then the Prosecution must put the nature of their case to the witness so that he can comment on the nature of that case. So that Your Honours, when Your Honours sit down to deliberate, can say, Well, yes, the witness did confirm the Prosecution case in relation to these aspects. When the Prosecution, however, put the nature of the case to him on the aspects which were contradicting their case, the witness was given an opportunity to respond and responded in this way. That gives the full contextualisation which will assist Your Honours to get towards the truth. The Prosecution are wanting, if I may use an English phrase, to have their cake and to eat it; not to comply with their obligations, but to adduce evidence which they later rely upon without giving the witness an opportunity to explain and deal with the contradictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's the Prosecutor's -- Prosecution's understanding from the Chamber's decision that the purpose of Rule 90(H) is to first ensure efficient and fair presentation of the evidence, to -- second, to assist the Trial Chamber in judging the credibility of the witness, and, third, protect the witness from confusion. During today's examination, the Prosecution started by attempting to challenge the -- both the bias of the witness and then also the intent that the witness specifically had during his time as a member of the Serbian Volunteer Guard. The witness has offered during his evidence broad testimony that the Serbian MUP had nothing to do with the Serbian Volunteer Guard. That including the Serbian DB. The Prosecution throughout their examination today did attempt to challenge whether or not, in fact, that was true. For example, we confronted the witness with the decision about Badza's appointment and the fact that he was actually a minister at the time. We challenged the witness in terms of how checks were done. Things of this nature. We did so in the context of trying to ascertain what the witness's knowledge actually was, whether he had participated in earlier operations very similar to many of the -- well, Your Honours further explored that on -- on examination, whether or not he knew or was part of operations in Zvornik or Bijeljina, how many convoys that he was a part of, and whether he deployed during other times to which he offers generalised evidence about the lack of DB involvement. In the context of what is fair to the witness, I believe it is -- the Prosecution has sufficiently met its burden pursuant to Rule 90(H) in terms of trying to confront the witness and also establish what his knowledge actually is and is not, and also attempting to establish any biases or interests that he may have. With respect to Mr. Jordash's points, that the Prosecution will later contest the case by challenging the credibility of the witness and whether or not during examination we put the Prosecution's case in general or specific, while he is cross-referencing the documents that the Prosecution used that were produced from the Simatovic Defence, we'll address this altogether, since that is an example. The Prosecution received through the disclosure of the Simatovic Defence documents that were produced by this very witness. So the documents do relate directly to what the witness had in his possession and what he may know or not know. The witness, during the examination today, at page 124, indicated that these documents came directly from Arkan's drawer. Prior to this, the Prosecution examined on who these individuals were and what the extent of the witness's knowledge was or was not about these individuals and their relationship to the Serbian Volunteer Guard. Towards the end of this examination, I asked the witness whether or not he knew definitively that the people were members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard and whether or not they could have worked for any other organisation other than the Serbian Volunteer Guard. With respect to the four individuals who are deceased, all four of these individuals appear on Serbian DB payment records at the exact time that they, according to these records, that they were killed. We do intend to later make submissions on this, and it does relate to what the witness knew or may not have known that was in Arkan's own very drawer. So that is a example of documents that were directly produced by this witness, that he had in his possession for a very long period of time, that he has now brought to this court. They were not people that we focussed on during the course of presenting our evidence, but since the document's directly related to this witness and what he had and where he got it from, the Prosecution did examine on that, and also sought to tendered the documents because it appears, according to at least what the witness offered as an answer, that he didn't know whether or not they worked for any other organisation. We do tend to later compare that to payment records that we have admitted that show that these individuals were paid by another organisation, that being the Serbian DB. So, in our submission, we met our burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. The indictment, paragraph 12, places Arkan as a member of the plurality with Stanisic. The Prosecution's case is that Stanisic and -- was in control of Arkan. The indictment at paragraph 42 and 43 has Arkan and special units of the DB involved in that attack. Zvornik, paragraph 57, the same. We have, as the core part of the Prosecution case, the DB and Stanisic and Arkan as close collaborators. This witness could never, from Mr. Weber's cross-examination, have discerned that. It is very telling, in our submission, that the Prosecution can cross-examine a witness of this potential significance and not provide any indication to the witness of that case. Now, what, instead, they do, is they go through the back door. They move around the subject. They put documents to the witness but don't tell him why. If they say this witness - and my learned friend has just said that they intend to make submissions basically about this witness's credibility, about his knowledge about the DB and Arkan, by linking these five men with DB payment records, and then they'll make a submission at the end and say, See, this witness was lying. So isn't it fair that they put that to the witness? The DB, the payment lists, the men, let's find out what the witness has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weber, any need to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just respond to that last point by saying that Mr. Jordash, in his submission on point 4, said whether or not we put it to the witness in any general or specific form. And we believe we have, by asking the witness whether or not he worked for any -- those individuals worked for any other organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the witness didn't know, isn't it? That was his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, part of the witness's testimony also was that there were no links to the MUP. Why didn't you put the payment lists to the witness, which would -- I mean, if you say there's no link, that's more or less denying the case of the Prosecution, to say, Well, if I would show you payment lists on which the individuals you brought us papers about are reported as having received money, who -- that would be -- the witness may have a good answer to that, isn't it? That this money was -- that the lists are forgeries or that ... whatever. Or that they got paid for -- for other reasons or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, I'd be happy to follow whatever the Chamber guidance is; however, the witness is making blanket denials that he never had anything to do with the DB, that he had never had any part of the DB, and I challenged that. Now to show him documents that come from the DB, I'm not sure if that's his position, what type of credible answer -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever say, It's our case that there was a link with the DB? because that is what Mr. Jordash is asking you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not whether you're willing to follow my suggestion. We are in a legal debate at this moment. Mr. Jordash says under the Rules you should have told the witness, It's our case that there was a link with the DB. Even to say more: that there was a link with Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Stanisic. That's ... if I understood you well, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's ... let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will further consider the matter. And nevertheless, the Chamber will ask two or three questions to the witness on the matter. And the parties should not misunderstood this. This is it purely to avoid that once we finally made up our minds on the debate -- the issue in debate between the parties, that the witness would be away and we could not even possibly ask him any further questions about it. Therefore, and I'll put those questions to the witness very briefly. And, again, it will be about putting a case to the witness. Because one of the concerns is that the witness may be confused. And if at a later stage we have to say, "Well, we did not know whether the witness understood certain things, yes or no," then it's very difficult to then establish whether he did or not. Again, that's a step we'll take at this moment. But it does not in any way anticipate what our final ruling on the debate will be. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 7.00. I'm looking at the clock. I even have an urgent other matter to deal with. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just wanted to note that although we've been discussing five names on specific documents, the witness did mention a lot of individuals throughout the course of his testimony that do appear on the payment records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The more reason to put to him that you find them on payment lists, isn't it? Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. I said I would read another decision. We will not find time for that. At the same time, the Chamber wants the parties to be informed about that statement. If I said a decision, that's wrong. It's a statement. It's a statement on bar table motions by the Stanisic Defence. We'll just do not find time to read it. It is there, however, in written form. I will put it on the record at a later stage as reading. But a courtesy copy, which is very uncommon, will be provided in order to avoid that the parties will be ignorant until next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, I have a few questions for you. You're still bound by the solemn declaration. Further Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware that it is the Prosecution's case that the SDG, Arkan's men, did have a link with the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia, that there were links? Did you know that that is what the Prosecution's case is? Not whether you agree with that, but did you know that that is what the Prosecution puts here? Are -- were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I realized that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You realized that. Were you also aware that, in this context, that the Prosecution alleges and it's the Prosecution's case that it was not only a link with the Serbian MUP, but that that included direct involvement of Mr. Simatovic and Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I realized that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would your answers -- apparently you are aware of that. I will now put a different matter to you. A few individuals were discussed. We have seen personal documents with the small photographs, the ones you gave to the Simatovic Defence. Apart from other prominent SDG members, four or five members were discussed. You remember that, the documents you gave and the reports on who died where and when? Yes. Now, it's the Prosecution's case that they were paid by the -- by the RDB of Serbia, the Ministry of the Interior, and in this case we have seen payment lists on which names appear. Now, on the assumption that the persons we discussed appear on these payment lists, and it is the Prosecution's case that they were paid by the Serbian -- by the MUP Serbia, would that have -- first of all, are you aware that such payment lists do exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would it have influenced your answer in any way if the Prosecution would have told you, "Well, talking about these people who died at certain dates in a certain context --" if the Prosecution would have told you that the names of those persons appear on those payment lists, would you have had an explanation for that, or would that have in any way influenced your answer, the answers you gave?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I noticed that these individuals were killed in the Banja Luka Krajina; namely, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and Novi Grad. They were called by Fikret Abdic, and I said as much. He was supposed to be paying them. If he was working for the RDB, then that's something I don't know. What I do know is that he took upon himself to pay the per diems, not their wages, but to pay the per diems of the members of the SDG for that short period that they spent training his soldiers. That is what Milan Milovanovic, aka Mrgud, told us, i.e., that the instructions -- instructors of the SDG were financed by Abdic. What the arrangements were, I don't know. But since I was in charge of the finances within the Guard, I know that not a single penny had arrived from the MUP of Serbia or the DB to the seat of the Guard in that period of time. Our instructors were receiving the per diems that I mentioned during their stay in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I think I have put the most salient parts of the Prosecution's case to the witness in order to find out. Whatever we'll do with the evidence, but whether there was a confusion on the witness's side. If there's anything you would like to suggest to in addition put to him, I'm trying to keep peace with everyone, because we are already at eight minutes past 7.00. If there's an important matter you think should be added, then we should do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I just ask a couple of questions? I think I might be able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then I have to -- I shouldn't have promised anything to the witness. Could you do it in two minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two minutes. I'm looking at the interpreters. I know that I'm not -- I wished I would not be in this position at this moment. Mr. Jordash, two minutes. And I'll be strict.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So, from what you've said, as far as you're aware, finances were coming from Abdic to Arkan's men who were taking part in Pauk, and you know that because the -- the -- the paper administration recording that payment came through you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So if some of Arkan's men were receiving payments from the DB, as far as you're concerned that was outside of the normal financial administration of the Arkan's Tigers, something perhaps more personal between individuals, agreement between individuals from the DB and Arkan -- and a select few of Arkan's men? Do you understand my point?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do understand it. However, I assert that there had never been any sort of deals or negotiations between Arkan and a few -- and a select few, as you put it, because it had -- it would had to have gone through me. What I state is that our instructors received their payment through the units in the field, and not from the Guards' staff. And I said that this conversation between Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the names that he just mentioned. It was too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please -- the conversation between Milosevic and ... And could you then continue your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The conversation between Milosevic, Karadzic, Martic, and Fikret Abdic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm happy to leave it there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're happy to leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by this Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. We adjourn. And we will resume -- no, before -- one final observation. The Chamber will consider the proposal made and where the parties apparently do not disagree, and we'll later deal with any documents which the parties intended to tender but which they have not yet tendered yet, and the statement which the parties need in order not to -- to have problems in the near future, and the time-limits in there will be available after Court and will be read into the record at a later stage. We adjourn. And we will resume Tuesday, the 31st of January, at 9.00 in the morning in this same courtroom, II. And I apologise to the interpreters and all those assisting us.
